title: Containers with NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=all fail to start in jit-cdi mode when every GPU is bound to vfio-pci
error_message: failed to create the automatic CDI modifier: failed to generate CDI spec for mode "auto": failed to construct device spec generators: failed to initialize NVML: No supported GPUs were found
description:
**Describe the bug**

When every GPU on a node is bound to `vfio-pci` (driver loaded, no GPU bound to it), the `nvidia` runtime in jit-cdi mode fails to create containers with `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=all`:

    failed to create the automatic CDI modifier: failed to generate CDI spec for mode "auto": failed to construct device spec generators: failed to initialize NVML: No supported GPUs were found

This happens with the NVIDIA DRA driver's `PassthroughSupport`: while every GPU is in a KubeVirt VM, GPU Operator operands (gpu-feature-discovery, dcgm-exporter) cannot be recreated on that node.

`nvmllib.DeviceSpecGenerators` (`pkg/nvcdi/lib-nvml.go`) calls `nvmlInit` before handling `all`, and the init fails when no GPU is bound.

**Expected behavior**

`all` with no GPUs available resolves to no devices, as `none` does, and the container starts. I can send a PR.

**Environment**
- nvidia-container-toolkit v1.19.1 (same code on `main`), driver 595.91.07
- Talos v1.14.2, kernel 6.18.54, containerd 2.3.6, Kubernetes v1.37.1
- RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell × 2, GPU Operator v26.7.1, DRA driver v0.5.1, KubeVirt v1.9.0

title: libnvsdm missing from management CDI specs
error_message: ERROR [316:316] [[NvSwitch]] NVSDM error: 8 [./modules/nvswitch/DcgmNvsdmManager.cpp:982]
missing_evidence: toolkit_version, driver_version, cuda_version, os_info, container_runtime, nvidia_smi_output
description:
## Summary

On HGX B200/B300 nodes with 5th-generation NVLink, which use NVSDM instead of NSCQ for NVSwitch telemetry, the management CDI spec doesn't mount `libnvsdm.so.1` or the libraries it depends on into management containers. NVSDM initialization then fails inside DCGM, and NVSwitch metrics are not collected.

## Background

- Earlier generations used `libnvidia-nscq.so.<major>.<minor>.<patch>`. Its filename carries the driver version, so the driver-library discoverer, which matches on the driver version suffix, picked it up.
- B200/B300 uses NVSDM. Its library is `libnvsdm.so.1`, with no driver version in the name, so the version-suffix match never finds it.
- `libnvsdm.so.1` depends on `libibumad.so.3`and `libibmad.so.5`.

## Steps to reproduce

1. HGX B200 node, 5th-gen NVLink, NVIDIA driver installed.
2. Generate the management CDI spec (`management.nvidia.com/gpu`) with the toolkit -- `sudo nvidia-ctk cdi generate --mode management --output /var/run/cdi/management.nvidia.com-gpu.yaml`
3. Launch DCGM container with access to `management.nvidia.com/gpu=all`.

## Expected behavior

DCGM is able to initialize NVSDM and collect NVSwitch metrics.

## Actual behavior

NVSDM initialization fails inside DCGM and NVSwitch metrics are not collected. We see the following logs in the DCGM container:

```
level=INFO msg="Not collecting NvSwitch metrics; no switches to monitor"
```

When enabling debug logs with `nv-hostengine` we see:
```
ERROR [316:316] [[NvSwitch]] NVSDM error: 8 [./modules/nvswitch/DcgmNvsdmManager.cpp:982]
```

title: nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker without --set-as-default leaves default-runtime set to nvidia
missing_evidence: toolkit_version, driver_version, cuda_version, os_info, gpu_model, error_or_logs, nvidia_smi_output
description:
**Describe the bug**

#1256 (cab76e2d) changed `AddRuntime` for containerd and cri-o to clear the default runtime when the runtime being added is the current default and `setAsDefault` is false. The docker implementation in `pkg/config/engine/docker/docker.go` was not changed: it only sets `default-runtime` when `setAsDefault` is true and leaves an existing value alone otherwise.

So after the NVIDIA runtime was made the docker default once (`--set-as-default`, or the toolkit container with set-as-default enabled), configuring it again with set-as-default off keeps `"default-runtime": "nvidia"` in `daemon.json`, and every docker container keeps running through the NVIDIA runtime. With the same steps, containerd and cri-o go back to their own default.

**To Reproduce**

Found by reading the code and confirmed with a unit test on main (44f1c6ef): `Config{"default-runtime": "nvidia"}.AddRuntime("nvidia", path, false)` leaves `default-runtime` as `nvidia`.

Expected on a host (not run):

1. `nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker --set-as-default`
2. `nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker`
3. `/etc/docker/daemon.json` still has `"default-runtime": "nvidia"`.

**Expected behavior**

Docker behaves like containerd and cri-o: when the runtime being configured is the current default and set-as-default is off, `default-runtime` is removed and docker falls back to its own default (runc).

One thing for the maintainers to decide: this changes behaviour for anyone who set `default-runtime: nvidia` by hand and later runs `nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker` without `--set-as-default`. That is the same trade-off #1256 made for containerd and cri-o, but it may matter more for docker users. A fix that mirrors #1256 is in #2156.

**Environment (please provide the following information):**
 - NVIDIA Container Toolkit version: main at 44f1c6ef; the same code is in v1.20.1
 - NVIDIA Driver Version, host OS, kernel, container runtime: not run on a host; reproduced with the `pkg/config/engine/docker` unit tests (Go 1.27.2, macOS arm64)

title: Containerized installer removes the existing Toolkit installation before the replacement is complete and durable
error_message: Containers using the affected NVIDIA runtime cannot start if required runtime files are missing or unusable. If NVIDIA is the default runtime, non-GPU containers can also be affected.
description:
**_Important Note: NVIDIA AI Enterprise customers can get support from NVIDIA Enterprise support. Please open a case_** [**_here_**](<https://enterprise-support.nvidia.com/s/create-case>)_._

**Describe the bug**

The containerized Toolkit installer deletes the existing installation directory, typically `/usr/local/nvidia/toolkit`, before preparing its replacement. It then writes the new files directly into the live directory.

The file-writing code uses `os.Create`, `io.Copy`, permission updates, and a deferred `Close`. It does not explicitly sync the installed files and directories to disk before returning success. Errors from the deferred `Close` are also not checked.

This creates two failure windows:

- **Installation fails or is interrupted:** The previous installation has already been deleted, but the replacement is incomplete. A reboot that interrupts installation during this window can leave required runtime files missing or unusable. This does not require a loss of buffered writes.
- **Power loss or hard reset before writes reach disk:** Even after the write operations return successfully, data may still be in memory. After reboot, installed files may be missing, incomplete, or zero-length, depending on filesystem and writeback timing.

Containers using the affected NVIDIA runtime cannot start if required runtime files are missing or unusable. If NVIDIA is the default runtime, non-GPU containers can also be affected.

If the Toolkit installer Pod itself uses the same NVIDIA runtime, it also cannot restart to repair those files, creating a circular dependency that prevents automatic recovery.

Relevant code at commit `3e112b4af299bf72a1b23193b4f5c3321475dd6d`:

- [`Installer.Install`](<https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/blob/3e112b4af299bf72a1b23193b4f5c3321475dd6d/cmd/nvidia-ctk-installer/toolkit/toolkit.go#L291>) deletes the existing installation before installing its replacement.
- [`installContentStub`](<https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/blob/3e112b4af299bf72a1b23193b4f5c3321475dd6d/cmd/nvidia-ctk-installer/toolkit/installer/installer.go#L153>) writes files without explicitly syncing them to disk.
- [`installToolkitConfig`](<https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/blob/3e112b4af299bf72a1b23193b4f5c3321475dd6d/cmd/nvidia-ctk-installer/toolkit/toolkit.go#L379>) also writes directly to the final configuration path and defers `Close`.

The same removal and file-writing patterns are present in the [v1.17.8 installer](<https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/blob/v1.17.8/tools/container/toolkit/toolkit.go#L294>).

Closing a file does not ensure its contents are persisted to disk. Directory entries also require synchronization; see [`fsync(2)`](<https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fsync.2.html>).

**To Reproduce**

The early-deletion behavior was reproduced with an isolated test using the installer API:

1. Create a temporary installation directory containing a nonempty placeholder `nvidia-container-runtime` file.
2. Create an installer with `WithToolkitRoot` pointing to that directory and `WithSourceRoot` pointing to a nonexistent source directory.
3. Call `Installer.Install(&cli.Command{}, &toolkit.Options{}, "containerd")`.
4. After installation returns an error, check whether the original file and directory still exist.

The installer returns an error because the source library cannot be found, but the previous installation directory and its contents have already been deleted. The test output is included below.

This test only operates on a temporary directory and verifies the early-deletion behavior. **The power-loss/zero-length-file scenario has not yet been reproduced in a controlled Linux crash-recovery test.**

**Expected behavior**

A failed or interrupted reinstall should preserve a complete, usable installation.

The replacement files and directories should be validated and durably written before replacing the active installation. Installation success should be reported only after the required file and directory updates have been persisted.

**Environment (please provide the following information):**

The following describes the standalone installer API test:

- `nvidia-container-toolkit` version: Source commit `3e112b4af299bf72a1b23193b4f5c3321475dd6d`. The corresponding installation logic was also reviewed in `v1.17.8`.
- NVIDIA Driver Version: N/A — no driver is used by this test.
- Host OS: macOS.
- Kernel Version: Not captured for the recorded test.
- Container Runtime Version: N/A — no running container runtime is required; `"containerd"` is passed as the installer API argument.
- CPU Architecture: `arm64`.
- GPU Model(s): N/A — no GPU is required.
- Kubernetes Distro and Version: N/A — the test runs outside Kubernetes.
- NVIDIA GPU Operator version: N/A.
- CUDA Version: N/A.

**Information to** [**attach**](<https://help.github.com/articles/file-attachments-on-issues-and-pull-requests/>)

Standalone test output:

```
install_returned_error: true
old_file_exists_after_failure: false
live_directory_exists_after_failure: false

error:
could not install toolkit components: failed to collect libraries:
error locating library: libnvidia-container.so.1: not found
```

`nvidia-smi` output and container logs are not applicable to this standalone test.
discussion:
Maybe we should make the Toolkit’s runtime installation and update process more atomic.

For example, copy the new runtime files from the container image into a staging directory first. Once they are ready, switch them into the live path using mv, replacing the old files. This would reduce the window where the old files have been deleted but the new files are not yet ready.

title: nvidia-container-runtime as low-level OCI runtime (BinaryName/PATH-shadow) breaks ALL container creation: fork/exec /proc/self/fd/N: permission denied
error_message: runc create failed: unable to start container process: unable to start
description:
**Describe the bug**

`nvidia-container-runtime` used as a drop-in low-level OCI runtime (i.e. as
`containerd-shim-runc-v2`'s `BinaryName`, replacing `runc` directly, not via
the Docker `--gpus`/CDI-annotation-on-create path) breaks container creation
deterministically with:

```
runc create failed: unable to start container process: unable to start
init: fork/exec /proc/self/fd/6: permission denied
```

This reproduces for **every** container through this configuration,
including containers with no NVIDIA env vars set and no GPU devices
requested at all (confirmed with a plain `busybox echo` and `nvidia/cuda
nvidia-smi`, both fail identically). `nvidia-container-runtime` delegates to
a real, working `runc` binary (confirmed working standalone via `--version`
and via a direct `ctr run --runc-binary <path>` invocation with no
`nvidia-container-runtime` in the chain). The failure only appears when
`nvidia-container-runtime` sits between the shim and that same delegate
runc.

This is not the known flaky fd-reuse race in
https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/issues/4294 (that one is described as
intermittent in runc's own test suite) -- this one is 100% deterministic
across 5/5 attempts, in both `mode = "auto"` and `mode = "legacy"`, and with
zero GPU involvement. `dmesg` shows no AppArmor/SELinux/seccomp denial at the
time of failure.

**To Reproduce**

Context: a privileged, `cgroup: host` container running its own embedded
`containerd` (Concourse CI's worker, but the mechanism is generic to any
nested-containerd-via-ctr setup), with CRI disabled
(`disabled_plugins = ["io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri", ...]`), driven directly
via the core containerd client / `ctr`, not CRI.

1. Inside that containerd's environment, locate the delegate runc the shim
   would normally use by default (no runtime options set): in this setup,
   `/usr/local/concourse/bin/runc` (the `concourse/concourse` image's own
   bundled, non-ABI-mismatched runc).
2. Copy it aside to a new path, e.g. `/opt/concourse-runc/runc` (confirmed
   `--version` works at the new path).
3. Point `nvidia-container-runtime`'s own config at that delegate:
   ```toml
   [nvidia-container-runtime]
   mode = "auto"   # reproduces identically with mode = "legacy"
   runtimes = ["/opt/concourse-runc/runc"]
   ```
4. Shadow the original path with `nvidia-container-runtime` itself (a plain
   bind mount, no containerd.toml change -- containerd's client issues
   `NewContainer` with no runtime options at all here, so the shim does a
   bare `$PATH` lookup for the literal name `runc`):
   ```
   -v /usr/bin/nvidia-container-runtime:/usr/local/concourse/bin/runc:ro
   -v ./concourse-runc/runc:/opt/concourse-runc/runc:ro
   ```
5. Create ANY container through this setup, with or without
   `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` set:
   ```
   ctr run --rm docker.io/library/busybox:latest test echo hi
   ```

Result: deterministic failure as above, every time, regardless of GPU
env vars.

**Expected behavior**

`nvidia-container-runtime` delegating to a working, correctly-pathed runc
binary should pass container creation through unmodified when no GPU
devices are requested (it does inject correctly when invoked via the normal
Docker `--gpus`/CRI RuntimeClass path on the same host -- `docker run --gpus
all` with this exact driver/toolkit version works fine). The failure appears
specific to being invoked as the shim's default low-level runtime (via
`BinaryName`/PATH shadowing) rather than via CRI or Docker's own
`--gpus` plumbing.

**Environment**

- `nvidia-container-toolkit` version: 1.20.1 (commit
  `dffc40b4f820ce5c512633bac9e0418d0e05a2ee`)
- NVIDIA Driver Version: 595.99.02
- Host OS: Linux Mint 22.3
- Kernel Version: 6.17.0-42-generic
- Container Runtime Version: containerd v2.3.3 (`aad11006b869517fcd3009450b6f82da282e1a9b`), runc 1.5.1 (delegate) / runc 1.5.2 (host, not used in this path)
- CPU Architecture: x86_64
- GPU Model: RTX 3090
discussion:
Could you run the following and report the result here?

1. Try bind-mounted runc directly, no `nvidia-container-runtime` involved:

   Use the bind-mounted `/opt/concourse-runc/runc` here, not `/usr/local/concourse/bin/runc`.

   ```
   ctr run --rm --runc-binary /opt/concourse-runc/runc docker.io/library/busybox:latest test echo hi
   ```

2. Mount the directory instead of the file:

   Replace

   `-v ./concourse-runc/runc:/opt/concourse-runc/runc:ro` with
   `-v ./concourse-runc:/opt/concourse-runc:ro`,

   then repeat step 1 and your original `nvidia-container-runtime` setup.

---COMMENT---

**1. File mount:**
```bash
docker run -d --rm --name ctd-repro2 --privileged --cgroupns=host \
  ... \
  -v /tmp/ctd-repro/concourse-runc/runc:/opt/concourse-runc/runc:ro \
  ... concourse/concourse --config /etc/containerd/config.toml

$ ctr run --rm --runc-binary /opt/concourse-runc/runc docker.io/library/busybox:latest test echo hi
ctr: failed to create shim task: OCI runtime create failed: runc create failed: unable to start container process: unable to start init: fork/exec /proc/self/fd/6: permission denied
```

**2. Same recipe, that one line swapped to a directory mount:**
```bash
docker run -d --rm --name ctd-repro2 --privileged --cgroupns=host \
  ... \
  -v /tmp/ctd-repro/concourse-runc:/opt/concourse-runc:ro \
  ... concourse/concourse --config /etc/containerd/config.toml

$ ctr run --rm --runc-binary /opt/concourse-runc/runc docker.io/library/busybox:latest test echo hi
hi
```

**3. Original `nvidia-container-runtime` setup, only that same mount changed — `nvidia-container-runtime` itself still file-mounted, unchanged from the original report:**
```bash
docker run -d --rm --name ctd-repro2 --privileged --cgroupns=host \
  ... \
  -v /tmp/ctd-repro/concourse-runc:/opt/concourse-runc:ro \
  -v /usr/bin/nvidia-container-runtime:/opt/runc-shadow/runc:ro \
  ... concourse/concourse --config /etc/containerd/config.toml

$ ctr run --rm --runc-binary /opt/runc-shadow/runc --env NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=all docker.io/nvidia/cuda:12.6.0-base-ubuntu22.04 test nvidia-smi
Thu Oct 22 05:42:13 2026
... RTX 3090, driver 595.99.02, CUDA 13.2 ...
```

D'oh! So I was holding `runc` wrong and just happened to do so in the vicinity of `nvidia-container-toolkit`. 🤦🏼‍♂️  Thanks for your help!

title: nvidia-cdi-hook chmod: adopt os.Root confinement like sibling hooks
missing_evidence: driver_version, cuda_version, os_info, gpu_model, repro_steps, nvidia_smi_output
description:
## Summary
`cmd/nvidia-cdi-hook/chmod/chmod.go` (reviewed at tag `v1.20.1`) resolves its target
paths with plain string concatenation (`filepath.Join(root, f)`) and then calls
`os.Stat` (`getPaths`, chmod.go:143-147) and `os.Chmod` (`run`, chmod.go:131)
directly on the resulting string. Every other root-executed, filesystem-writing hook
in the same binary already confines its path resolution:

| Hook | Confinement |
|---|---|
| `create-symlinks` | `pathrs.OpenatInRoot` / `MkdirAllHandle` (cyphar/filepath-securejoin/pathrs-lite) |
| `enable-cuda-compat` | `pathrs.OpenatInRoot` + `Openat(O_NOFOLLOW\|O_EXCL)` for writes |
| `disable-device-node-modification` | `os.OpenRoot` |
| `update-application-profile` | `os.OpenRoot` |
| `update-ldcache` | `pivot_root` into the container root |
| **`chmod`** | **none** — `filepath.Join` + `os.Stat` + `os.Chmod` |

The chmod hook is the only hook in this family without root confinement, which makes
it structurally inconsistent with the hardening applied after CVE-2024-0132 /
CVE-2025-23359 / CVE-2026-24260.

## Lab verification (no security issue observed)
To be explicit: **I tested this end-to-end and found no currently-reachable security
problem.** In a real podman + crun pipeline (crun 1.30.1, toolkit v1.20.1, CDI spec
generated with `--enable-hooks chmod` and `--path /dev/dri` added to the hook args to
mirror the spec shape produced when a hooked folder is present):

- A container image **can** carry an absolute symlink at `/dev/dri` via an `ADD`
  tarball (it survives into the image layer and the extracted rootfs; `RUN ln -s`
  does not survive, since build-time changes under `/dev` are not committed).
- However, crun populates the container rootfs `/dev` with its own tmpfs *before*
  the `createContainer` hook runs, so the image-supplied symlink is not visible at
  hook time. The hook's own debug log confirms it skips the path:
  `Skipping path ".../rootfs/dev/dri": stat ... no such file or directory`.

So this is a **defensive consistency request, not a vulnerability report**. The
observed runtime behavior masks the issue; the request is to not rely on that
masking.

## Request
Rework `getPaths()` to use the pattern the sibling hooks already use (the module
already pins `go 1.26.0`, so `os.Root` is available), e.g.:

```go
root, err := os.OpenRoot(containerRoot)
if err != nil { return err }
defer root.Close()

for _, p := range paths {
    if _, err := root.Stat(p); errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist) {
        continue
    }
    f, err := root.OpenFile(p, os.O_RDONLY, 0)
    if err != nil { /* skip, as today */ }
    if err := f.Chmod(mode); err != nil { /* skip, as today */ }
    f.Close()
}
```

This makes the hook robust against the symlink-following class of bugs by
construction, instead of relying on the runtime's `/dev` tmpfs masking, and keeps
this file consistent with the rest of the hook family.

## Notes
- The hook is marked deprecated; simply removing it would also resolve the
  inconsistency.
- `--mode 755` and the hooked-folder allowlist (`/dev/dri`, `/dev/nvidia-caps`) are
  hardcoded in the generator (`pkg/nvcdi/workarounds-device-folder-permissions.go`),
  so the current blast radius is narrow — another reason this is a consistency ask
  rather than a security fix.
discussion: Update on this hardening request: the reachability question is now settled empirically on my side. With an image that declares an image volume at `/dev` (carrying `/dev/dri` or `/dev/nvidia-caps` as an absolute symlink), Docker mounts the image-populated volume at `/dev` instead of the default tmpfs, so the symlink is visible to the hook at createContainer time and the host target gets chmodded to 0755 (verified end-to-end in a disposable VM with the real v1.20.1 hook binary; same rootfs without the volume is unaffected). The related private report was closed as a duplicate, so this public note only records the reachability confirmation — no new submission is intended here. The suggested fix (os.OpenRoot confinement like the sibling hooks, or removing the deprecated hook) stands.

title: CDI spec WriteTo leaks the temporary descriptor on save errors
error_message: On current `main` (`023f35906ee23384b48dc3db3f2d1fb75d29f6b0`), eight failed writes leave eight open, deleted `nvcdi-spec-*.yaml` descriptors when garbage collection is disabled. This affects callers that reuse the public library after a validation or filesystem error.
missing_evidence: toolkit_version, driver_version, cuda_version, os_info, container_runtime, gpu_model, nvidia_smi_output
description:
**Describe the bug**

`spec.Interface.WriteTo` leaves the temporary file descriptor open when saving the CDI specification fails. The temporary pathname is removed, but the descriptor is only reclaimed by Go's file finalizer.

On current `main` (`023f35906ee23384b48dc3db3f2d1fb75d29f6b0`), eight failed writes leave eight open, deleted `nvcdi-spec-*.yaml` descriptors when garbage collection is disabled. This affects callers that reuse the public library after a validation or filesystem error.

**To Reproduce**

Run the following from a module that imports the toolkit:

```go
package main

import (
    "io"
    "runtime/debug"

    "github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/pkg/nvcdi/spec"
)

func main() {
    debug.SetGCPercent(-1) // Make descriptor cleanup independent of finalizers.
    s, err := spec.New(spec.WithVersion("invalid"))
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    for i := 0; i < 8; i++ {
        _, err := s.WriteTo(io.Discard)
        if err == nil {
            panic("expected CDI validation failure")
        }
    }
    select {} // Inspect /proc/<pid>/fd in another terminal.
}
```

Each failed write reports `failed to write spec: invalid CDI Spec: invalid version "invalid"`. `/proc/<pid>/fd` contains eight temporary CDI files with the `(deleted)` suffix. No temporary pathname remains on disk.

**Expected behavior**

Every return from `WriteTo` should close the temporary file descriptor, including failures before the existing explicit `tmpFile.Close()` call. The original save error and temporary-file cleanup should be preserved.

**Environment**

- Toolkit: current main at `023f35906ee23384b48dc3db3f2d1fb75d29f6b0`
- Linux amd64, Go 1.26.0
- Reproduction uses the public Go API; GPU, driver, and container-runtime operations are not involved.

**Additional information**

The error is reproducible without GPU hardware. I plan to add a focused regression that separately checks open descriptors and remaining temporary files, and ensure the temporary descriptor is closed on the save-error path.

title: Same package versions published as different .deb files in the CUDA repository and nvidia.github.io, so apt reinstalls them in a loop
description:
The container toolkit packages are published in two NVIDIA apt repositories: the toolkit's own (https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/stable/deb/amd64) and the CUDA network repository (https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/debian13/x86_64). For the same version, the two .deb files differ: the CUDA repository's copy carries an extra ar member, `_gpgbuilder` (an embedded signature), so its size and checksums differ, while `control.tar.xz` and `data.tar.xz` are byte-identical.

Checked on 2026-10-11 for libnvidia-container1, libnvidia-container-tools, nvidia-container-toolkit-base and nvidia-container-toolkit, versions 1.20.1-1 and 1.20.0-1: all eight pairs have different SHA256 sums. For example, libnvidia-container1 1.20.1-1 is 1236052 bytes with SHA256 9d803cd9c898… from nvidia.github.io, and 1237398 bytes with SHA256 6c968fc75aa5… from the CUDA repository.

What happens: apt treats the two files as two builds of the same version. The installed package carries no origin in dpkg's status, so apt associates it with one of them, here always the CUDA repository's, even right after installing the nvidia.github.io build. When nvidia.github.io has the higher pin, apt plans to install that build again at every upgrade, reported as a downgrade, and installing it does not end the loop: `apt full-upgrade` keeps showing "4 downgraded" on a machine that uses both CUDA and the container toolkit.

To reproduce (Debian 13 or 14, amd64): enable both repositories, install nvidia-container-toolkit, pin nvidia.github.io above developer.download.nvidia.com (for example 1003 and 1002), then run `apt-get -s full-upgrade`, install, and run it again.

Expected: one version, one file. Possible fixes on your side: publish the same .deb (same checksum) in both repositories, keep the toolkit in only one of them, or give the CUDA repository's builds a distinct version (for example a `+cuda` suffix) so apt can tell them apart.

A workaround that works here: package-specific pins giving both origins the same priority below 1000, so the newer version wins from either repository and an identical version never flips.

```
Package: libnvidia-container1 libnvidia-container-tools nvidia-container-toolkit nvidia-container-toolkit-base
Pin: origin nvidia.github.io
Pin-Priority: 990

Package: libnvidia-container1 libnvidia-container-tools nvidia-container-toolkit nvidia-container-toolkit-base
Pin: origin developer.download.nvidia.com
Pin-Priority: 990
```

Environment: Debian testing (forky), apt 3.3.3, toolkit 1.20.1-1.

This issue was written with AI assistance, which I directed and checked.

Daniel Campos Ramos

title: containerd cleanup removes imports for unrelated drop-ins
description:
**Describe the bug**

Removing the NVIDIA containerd drop-in can also remove an import used by unrelated drop-ins. With a top-level config containing only `version` and a single `imports = [".../conf.d/*.toml"]`, `ConfigWithDropIn.Save` removes that glob when its NVIDIA destination becomes empty. It does not check whether the glob still imports other files. The top-level config is then deleted as well.

An unrelated `conf.d/10-custom.toml` remains byte-for-byte unchanged on disk, but `containerd config dump` no longer loads its settings. For example, a custom debug level silently reverts to containerd's default. This affects the file-loaded cleanup path used by the installer's `Options.Unconfigure`, including a file config source. It does not require an empty `--drop-in-config` value.

**To Reproduce**

On `main` at `a672e378ef91bea7dfe92c0ed274847fa1cb9236`, use an isolated directory; no daemon restart is needed:

```sh
fixture=$(mktemp -d)
mkdir -p "$fixture/conf.d"
cat > "$fixture/config.toml" <<EOF
version = 3
imports = ["$fixture/conf.d/*.toml"]
EOF
cat > "$fixture/conf.d/10-custom.toml" <<'EOF'
[debug]
level = "debug"
EOF
cat > "$fixture/conf.d/99-nvidia.toml" <<'EOF'
[plugins."io.containerd.cri.v1.runtime".containerd.runtimes.nvidia]
runtime_type = "io.containerd.runc.v2"
EOF
containerd --config "$fixture/config.toml" config dump
```

The dump includes `level = 'debug'`. Run the existing file-loaded installer cleanup API from the toolkit checkout:

```sh
cat > "$fixture/cleanup.go" <<'EOF'
package main

import (
    "os"
    "path/filepath"

    "github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/cmd/nvidia-ctk-installer/container"
    "github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/pkg/config/engine/containerd"
)

func main() {
    root := os.Args[1]
    options := container.Options{
        TopLevelConfigPath: filepath.Join(root, "config.toml"),
        DropInConfig: filepath.Join(root, "conf.d", "99-nvidia.toml"),
        RuntimeName: "nvidia",
    }
    cfg, err := containerd.New(containerd.WithTopLevelConfigPath(options.TopLevelConfigPath))
    if err != nil { panic(err) }
    if err := options.Unconfigure(cfg); err != nil { panic(err) }
}
EOF
go run "$fixture/cleanup.go" "$fixture"
ls "$fixture/conf.d"
containerd --config "$fixture/config.toml" config dump
```

Cleanup succeeds. `99-nvidia.toml` and `config.toml` are deleted. `10-custom.toml` still exists with its original contents, but the second dump no longer includes the custom debug level.

I reproduced the same result with config version 2 and its `io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri` plugin name. Controls with only the NVIDIA drop-in clean up as expected; controls with multiple import patterns or another top-level setting retain their custom drop-in settings.

**Expected behavior**

Cleanup should remove NVIDIA runtime configuration while preserving import patterns that still load other drop-ins and preserving unrelated settings. Removing the top-level file remains reasonable when the shared glob has no other matching drop-ins and the file contains no other settings.

The relevant simplification is in `pkg/config/engine/containerd/config_drop_in.go`, specifically `topLevelConfig.removeImports` and `removeVersion`. A focused fix can keep the import when other matching drop-ins remain, using the local drop-in directory when host/container paths differ.

**Environment**

- NVIDIA Container Toolkit: source `main`, `a672e378ef91bea7dfe92c0ed274847fa1cb9236`
- Container runtime: containerd 2.2.1, using its real `config dump` parser
- Host OS: Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS
- Kernel: 5.15.0-191-generic
- CPU architecture: x86_64
- Driver / GPU: 595.91.07 / RTX 5060 Ti; this reproduction only reads isolated configuration files and does not exercise GPU execution or restart a containerd daemon

title: create-symlinks and update-ldcache hooks fail container create when the container rootfs is read-only
error_message: Error: container create failed: error executing hook `/usr/local/nvidia/toolkit/nvidia-cdi-hook` (exit code: 1)
description:
### Problem

Both `create-symlinks` and `update-ldcache` write into the container root filesystem. When that filesystem is read-only, the write fails with `EROFS`, the hook exits 1, and container creation is aborted:

```
Error: container create failed: error executing hook `/usr/local/nvidia/toolkit/nvidia-cdi-hook` (exit code: 1)
```

This is the same class of problem as #2026, which was fixed in v1.20.1 for `update-application-profile` by ignoring read-only filesystem errors. The other two hooks still abort.

Generalized: a CDI hook whose only effect is to modify the container root filesystem should not prevent the container from starting when that filesystem is read-only.

### Steps to reproduce

```console
$ podman run --rm --device <cdi-device> --read-only nvidia/cuda:12.6.3-base-ubuntu22.04 nvidia-smi
Error: OCI runtime error: crun: error executing hook `/usr/local/nvidia/toolkit/nvidia-cdi-hook` (exit code: 1)

$ podman run --rm --device <cdi-device> --read-only --tmpfs /etc --tmpfs /usr/lib64 nvidia/cuda:12.6.3-base-ubuntu22.04 nvidia-smi
# succeeds
```

Making both `/etc` and `/usr/lib64` writable is required; making either one writable on its own still fails. Those are the two paths the generated spec's hooks write to:

```yaml
- path: /usr/local/nvidia/toolkit/nvidia-cdi-hook
  args: [nvidia-cdi-hook, create-symlinks, --link, libEGL_nvidia.so.595.58.03::/usr/lib64/libEGL_nvidia.so.0, ...]
- path: /usr/local/nvidia/toolkit/nvidia-cdi-hook
  args: [nvidia-cdi-hook, update-ldcache, --folder, /usr/lib64, --folder, /usr/lib64/vdpau]
```

### Impact

Kubernetes workloads that set `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` cannot use GPUs. This is a common hardening requirement, and it is enforced by policy on many clusters (for example OpenShift `restricted-v2` style baselines and Gatekeeper/Kyverno `psp-readonlyrootfilesystem` constraints), so it is not something the workload owner can simply turn off.

### Environment

- nvidia-container-toolkit v1.19.0, also reproduced on v1.17.8 with regenerated CDI specs
- CRI-O and podman/crun, OpenShift 4.x, NVIDIA GPU Operator v26.3.0
- Driver 595.58.03, H100 NVL

Skipping the ldcache update does not make the libraries unreachable: they are bind-mounted into directories glibc already searches by default.

I have a patch following the same approach as the #2026 fix and will open a PR.
discussion:
Additional data: a reproduction that needs no GPU, no container runtime and no CDI spec, which isolates the hooks from the runtime.

Create a bundle whose root is a genuine read-only mount and invoke the hook directly with the OCI state on stdin:

```bash
B=/var/tmp/hooktest/bundle
mkdir -p $B/rootfs/{usr/lib64,etc,sbin}
cp /sbin/ldconfig $B/rootfs/sbin/ldconfig
echo '{"ociVersion":"1.0.2","root":{"path":"'$B'/rootfs"},"process":{"args":["/bin/true"]}}' > $B/config.json
mount --bind $B/rootfs $B/rootfs && mount -o remount,ro,bind $B/rootfs

STATE='{"ociVersion":"1.0.2","id":"t","status":"created","pid":1,"bundle":"'$B'"}'
echo "$STATE" | nvidia-cdi-hook create-symlinks --link libcuda.so.1::/usr/lib64/libcuda.so
echo "$STATE" | nvidia-cdi-hook update-ldcache --folder /usr/lib64
```

Result is identical on v1.17.8 and v1.19.0, so this is not a regression introduced by the 1.18 `update-ldcache` change:

| hook | writable root | read-only root |
|---|---|---|
| `create-symlinks` | exit 0 | **exit 1** |
| `update-ldcache` | exit 0 | **exit 1** |

```
# create-symlinks, v1.19.0 and v1.17.8
failed to create link [libcuda.so.1 /usr/lib64/libcuda.so]: failed to create symlink:
symlink libcuda.so.1 .../rootfs/usr/lib64/libcuda.so: read-only file system

# update-ldcache, v1.19.0
Error updating ldcache: error mounting /proc: mkdirat proc: read-only file system

# update-ldcache, v1.17.8
Error updating ldcache: error mounting /proc: error creating directory: mkdir .../rootfs/proc: read-only file system
```

Note the `update-ldcache` failures above are from the released binaries, which create `proc` in the container root. `main` no longer does that (`maskPseudoFilesystems` skips a missing `proc`), so on `main` the first read-only write is `ensureLdsoconfFile`/`createLdsoconfdFile` under `/etc`. Both are Go-level writes wrapped with `%w`, which is what #2132 keys off.

### Why this is not reported more widely

Whether the hooks ever see a read-only rootfs depends on the runtime, not on the workload. On a stock OpenShift node the `createContainer` hooks run *before* the read-only remount is applied, so the hooks write into the still-writable upperdir and a `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` GPU pod starts normally.

Measured on OCP 4.19.26 / CRI-O 1.31.13 / crun 1.26 / driver 580.82.07, toolkit v1.17.8, CDI forced to `mode = "cdi"`. A single pod shows both facts at once: `/usr/lib64/libcuda.so` exists (the hook created it) while `/proc/mounts` reports `overlay / overlay ro` and `touch` is denied on `/`, `/etc` and `/usr/lib64`.

Where the rootfs *is* read-only at hook time, container creation aborts, and the hooks are then the only thing standing between a hardened workload and a working GPU. That asymmetry is the argument for tolerating `EROFS` rather than requiring every affected cluster to drop the hardening.

---COMMENT---

Root cause update, superseding my earlier analysis above.

The hooks are not at fault. crun before 1.26 remounted the rootfs read-only **before** running `createContainer` hooks, while runc does it after; NVIDIA filed this as containers/crun#1924 and it was fixed in containers/crun#1925 (crun 1.26, 2025-12-22). On a runtime that applies the remount after the hooks, a `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` GPU pod starts fine with CDI hooks running, confirmed on a crun 1.26 node.

Two corrections to what I wrote earlier:

- "The libraries remain reachable" is wrong. `create-symlinks` creates the `SONAME -> library` links for the injected driver libraries, so on a read-only root nothing can resolve `libcuda.so.1` regardless of image layout. Tolerating EROFS would start a container whose GPU is unusable and move the failure to the first CUDA call.
- A hook-side fallback (bind-mounting a generated `ld.so.cache`) does not help either: ldconfig records `dir/soname` and relies on the symlink it creates, so with a read-only library directory every entry dangles.

#2132 is therefore reduced to diagnostics: the hooks keep failing container creation, but the error now names the read-only rootfs and the runtime requirement (runc or crun >= 1.26) instead of a bare exit code 1.

For reference, OpenShift ships crun 1.23.1 through 4.20.16 and crun 1.26 from 4.20.17.

title: Toolkit omits glvnd EGL vendor manifest (10_nvidia.json): Vulkan fails with 'Found no drivers!' even with ICD mount + libegl1
error_message: ERROR: loader_scanned_icd_add: Could not get 'vkCreateInstance' via
description:
### Description

GPU containers started with `NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=graphics` (legacy mode, `--gpus all`) get the NVIDIA GL/Vulkan driver libraries mounted, but **libglvnd's EGL vendor manifest (`/usr/share/glvnd/egl_vendor.d/10_nvidia.json`) is never injected** when the container image does not already ship one. The Vulkan ICD manifest (`nvidia_icd.json`) is likewise omitted for images without a pre-existing ICD file — a gap already tracked for the ICD in #1559, but the EGL vendor manifest is a distinct file that no existing issue names.

Without `10_nvidia.json`, the failure is silent and misleading: `libGLX_nvidia.so.0` loads, `vk_icdGetInstanceProcAddr` resolves via dlsym, but the driver aborts during glvnd vendor enumeration and the Vulkan loader reports:

```
ERROR: loader_scanned_icd_add: Could not get 'vkCreateInstance' via
'vk_icdGetInstanceProcAddr' for ICD libGLX_nvidia.so.0
ERROR: vkCreateInstance: Found no drivers! (ERROR_INCOMPATIBLE_DRIVER)
```

The suggested fix in #1952 (`apt-get install libegl1`) does **not** help in this case: libegl1 makes the loader reach the driver library, but glvnd still has no NVIDIA vendor entry to dispatch to.

### Mechanism (strace evidence)

`strace -f -e trace=openat,ioctl` diff of `vulkaninfo --summary` in the working host environment vs. inside the container:

- **Working (manifest present):** the driver opens `/proc/driver/nvidia/params` (20 accesses) → `/dev/nvidiactl` → `/dev/nvidia0`, enumerates the GPU, and `vkCreateInstance` succeeds.
- **Failing (manifest absent):** the trace ends during the `egl_vendor.d` directory scan — only `50_mesa.json` is present — and the process exits **without ever opening `/dev/nvidiactl` or `/proc/driver/nvidia/params` (0 accesses)**. The driver aborts at vendor-discovery time, before any device interaction.

This is why the failure leaves no driver-side log and why adding devices/permissions (`--device /dev/nvidia-caps/*`, `--privileged`) changes nothing: the driver is never reached.

### To reproduce

Environment: driver installed via the official `.run` installer (userspace in standard multiarch paths), NVIDIA Container Toolkit 1.20.1, Docker with the `nvidia` runtime, legacy mode (`--gpus all`).

```bash
# image WITHOUT any pre-existing EGL vendor manifest or Vulkan ICD
docker build -t vk-minimal - <<'EOF'
FROM debian:trixie
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y libvulkan1 vulkan-tools libegl1 libxext6 libx11-6
EOF

docker run --rm --gpus all -e NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=all --device /dev/dri \
  vk-minimal vulkaninfo --summary
# → "Found no drivers!" / ERROR_INCOMPATIBLE_DRIVER

# the same container with both manifests bind-mounted from the host:
docker run --rm --gpus all -e NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=all --device /dev/dri \
  -v /etc/vulkan/icd.d/nvidia_icd.json:/etc/vulkan/icd.d/nvidia_icd.json:ro \
  -v /usr/share/glvnd/egl_vendor.d/10_nvidia.json:/usr/share/glvnd/egl_vendor.d/10_nvidia.json:ro \
  vk-minimal vulkaninfo --summary
# → GPU0 enumerated (NVIDIA), apiVersion 1.4.x, works
```

Note the `update-application-profile` hook (from #1939, shipped in 1.20.0) runs and creates `/etc/nvidia/nvidia-application-profiles-rc.d` in the container, so the hook path is active — it just does not cover the glvnd EGL vendor manifest (nor the Vulkan ICD, in legacy mode).

### Proposal

Extend the graphics-capability injection (legacy hook and/or the CDI/JIT-CDI spec generation) to also mount:

1. `/usr/share/glvnd/egl_vendor.d/10_nvidia.json` (libglvnd EGL vendor manifest)
2. the Vulkan ICD manifest `nvidia_icd.json` (from `/etc/vulkan/icd.d/` or `/usr/share/vulkan/icd.d/`, wherever the driver installer placed it)

whenever the `graphics` capability is requested and the target container image does not already provide them.

### Related work

- #1559 — Vulkan ICD injection gap (maintainer-recognized); #1952, #191 — same loader error, community fix `libegl1` (insufficient for this case).
- NixOS/nixpkgs#529876 and NixOS/nixpkgs#539636 — independently reported the same two-manifest gap in the NixOS CDI module and fixed it by mounting both manifests; worth cross-linking, as this affects any environment where the base image lacks the manifests.

### Environment

- Toolkit 1.20.1 (nvidia-ctk 1.20.1, commit dffc40b), legacy mode
- Driver installed via `.run` installer (userspace libs in standard multiarch paths)
- RTX 3080 Ti, driver 595.104.02, Vulkan apiVersion 1.4.329
- Kernel 7.0.14, unprivileged LXC host (no-cgroups = true; unrelated to the bug — reproduced identically with and without)

— Ruth (an AI agent assisted by a human operator).
discussion:
I've been digging into this and I think I've found the root cause.

**Summary**
`newGraphicsConfigsDiscoverer` (GLVND / EGL vendor manifest) uses a *single* locator, while `newVulkanConfigsDiscover` uses two:
- `internal/discover/graphics.go:83` — `shareConfigs` uses `locator: driver.Configs()`, `required: ["glvnd/egl_vendor.d/10_nvidia.json", ...]`
- `internal/discover/graphics.go:133` — `newVulkanConfigsDiscover` uses `locator: lookup.First(driver.Configs(), driver.Files())`

**Why one locator is not enough**
- `Driver.Configs()` (`internal/lookup/root/root.go:239`) searches `{driverRoot}/etc` + the XDG data dirs (`{driverRoot}/usr/local/share`, `{driverRoot}/usr/share`).
- `Driver.Files()` (`internal/lookup/root/root.go:218`) is created *without* search paths, so per `getSearchPrefixes()` (`pkg/lookup/file.go`) its only prefix is `{driverRoot}` itself — it resolves `{driverRoot}/glvnd/egl_vendor.d/10_nvidia.json`.

On a standard layout (`driverRoot=/`, manifests under `/usr/share`) `Configs()` finds it. But on a layout where the driver ships configs directly under the driver root — the same class of layout `newVulkanConfigsDiscover` explicitly supports for GKE ("the vulkan ICD files are at `{{ .driverRoot }}/vulkan`") — `Configs()` returns **no** candidates. `mountsToContainerPath.Mounts()` (`internal/discover/mounts-to-container-path.go`) then only logs `Missing <target>` and `continue`s, so the manifest is silently *not* mounted and no error surfaces — which matches the "silent and misleading" failure described here. The Vulkan discoverer handles this via the `Files()` fallback; the EGL/GLVND one does not. That asymmetry looks like the actual gap.

**Proposed fix**
Give `newGraphicsConfigsDiscoverer` the same fallback: `lookup.First(driver.Configs(), driver.Files())`, leaving `required` and `containerRoot` unchanged (so the container-side path `/usr/share/glvnd/egl_vendor.d/10_nvidia.json` is unchanged). This widens *discovery* only; it does not change where files are mounted.

Two questions before I start:
1. Does this match your understanding, or is there a reason the EGL discoverer intentionally uses only `Configs()` / an existing plan for this?
2. Could you share the `driverRoot` / driver installation layout of the reported environment (e.g. driver container, GPU Operator, GKE)? That would confirm whether the non-standard-layout path is the one being hit.

Happy to implement it with unit tests covering the driver-root layout if you agree.

title: an empty --drop-in-config overwrites the engine config with drop-in-only content
missing_evidence: toolkit_version, driver_version, cuda_version, os_info, gpu_model, nvidia_smi_output
description:
**Describe the bug**

An empty `--drop-in-config` writes drop-in-only content over the top-level engine config. For cri-o that means every runtime already in `crio.conf` is replaced by the nvidia one; for containerd it means the nvidia runtime does not end up anywhere, and the config gains an `imports` glob pointing at its own directory. Both report success and exit 0.

The empty value is not a nonsense input, it is the value the code uses for docker, and `validateFlags` does not reject it for the other engines. `docker.New` returns a plain in-place config, so nothing goes wrong there. `crio.New` seeds its destination with `toml.NewEmpty()` and `containerd.New` seeds it with only the CRI plugin section wrapped in `ConfigWithDropIn`, so for those two the destination is always a drop-in tree, while `getOutputConfigPath` falls back to the top-level path when the drop-in path is empty.

The installer has the same fallback in `Options.Flush`, and `RUNTIME_DROP_IN_CONFIG=""` reaches it, since the flag's value source is `os.LookupEnv`, which reports an empty variable as set. That is the obvious way to turn drop-ins off from the GPU Operator.

**To Reproduce**

cri-o. Starting from a config with another runtime in it:

```
$ cat crio.conf
[crio]
  [crio.runtime]
    default_runtime = "crun"
    [crio.runtime.runtimes]
      [crio.runtime.runtimes.crun]
        runtime_path = "/usr/bin/crun"
        runtime_type = "oci"

$ nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=crio --config=$PWD/crio.conf --drop-in-config=
INFO Wrote updated config to /tmp/dropin/crio.conf
INFO It is recommended that crio daemon be restarted.

$ cat crio.conf
[crio]

  [crio.runtime]

    [crio.runtime.runtimes]

      [crio.runtime.runtimes.nvidia]
        runtime_path = "/usr/bin/nvidia-container-runtime"
        runtime_type = "oci"
```

`default_runtime` and the crun definition are gone, so cri-o comes up with no default runtime.

containerd, starting from a v2 config with runc and a cni section:

```
$ nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=containerd --config=$PWD/config.toml --drop-in-config=
INFO Wrote updated config to /tmp/dropin/config.toml

$ head -2 config.toml
imports = ["/tmp/dropin/*.toml"]
version = 2

$ grep -c runtimes.nvidia config.toml
0
```

The original content survives here, but the nvidia runtime is not in the file at all, so `--runtime nvidia` and `RuntimeClass nvidia` fail. `ConfigWithDropIn.Save` writes the drop-in to the top-level path and then overwrites that same path with the top-level tree, which is also where the self-referential `imports` glob comes from.

With the default sentinel `--drop-in-config` both runtimes behave correctly, which is what isolates the empty value as the trigger.

**Expected behavior**

Either the empty value is rejected for containerd and cri-o, the way the docker combination is already rejected in `validateFlags`, or the engines honour it by using the source config as the destination when no drop-in is in play. The second is the better of the two, since `Options.Flush` in the installer has the identical fallback and would otherwise stay broken.

**Environment**

- `nvidia-container-toolkit` version: built from `main` at a672e378, and the paths are unchanged on the current tip
- Host OS: this was reproduced with `nvidia-ctk` built and run locally, not on a GPU node; the code path is the TOML config handling in `cmd/nvidia-ctk/runtime/configure/configure.go` and `pkg/config/engine/{crio,containerd}`, which does not touch the driver
- CPU Architecture: arm64

Happy to send a PR for whichever of the two shapes you prefer.
discussion:
I traced both the CLI and installer flows: an empty drop-in path still builds a drop-in-only destination, while the flush falls back to the top-level config. I will make the empty-path case update the loaded top-level config directly and add regression coverage for both paths, keeping the default drop-in behavior intact.

---COMMENT---

Hi! I’d like to contribute to this issue.

I have hands-on experience building backend services in Go, working with Linux-based infrastructure, and debugging production systems.

I’d be interested in investigating how the drop-in configuration interacts with the existing container engine configuration and identifying why certain settings are being overwritten.

I’ll review the current configuration handling, work on a fix that preserves existing settings where appropriate, and add regression tests to prevent similar issues.

Please let me know if this issue is available for contribution or if there are any specific design considerations I should follow.

Thanks!

title: nvidia-cdi-refresh.service restarts indefinitely while the driver cannot load — the 5-in-10s start limit never trips once an attempt takes over ~1 s
error_message: When the NVIDIA kernel module is installed but cannot bind the GPU until the next reboot, `nvidia-cdi-refresh.service` restarts indefinitely. On a first driver install, for example, `nouveau` still owns the device until the reboot. Every attempt runs `nvidia-smi -L`, which tries to load `nvidia.ko` and fails, so the host loads and fails the module about every 2.3 s.
description:
**Describe the bug**

When the NVIDIA kernel module is installed but cannot bind the GPU until the next reboot, `nvidia-cdi-refresh.service` restarts indefinitely. On a first driver install, for example, `nouveau` still owns the device until the reboot. Every attempt runs `nvidia-smi -L`, which tries to load `nvidia.ko` and fails, so the host loads and fails the module about every 2.3 s.

The unit intends to cap this: "Limit the number of successive restarts to 5 in 10 seconds." The cap only holds when a failed attempt takes under about 1 s, because systemd's start limit is a fixed window opened by the first start. In systemd's `ratelimit_below()` (`src/basic/ratelimit.c`, unchanged through v259), a start is refused only when the **6th** start lands within `StartLimitIntervalSec` of the window's first start. With `RestartSec=1s`, a cycle longer than 2.0 s means the 6th start opens a new window instead.

Here a failed attempt took about 1.3 s (`nvidia-smi -L` probing the device), so the cycle was about 2.3 s. The service ran **2,391 restarts over roughly 94 minutes**. The limit ("Start request repeated too quickly") tripped only when jitter happened to fit six starts into one 10 s window. Until then each cycle added:

```
NVIDIA-SMI has failed because it couldn't communicate with the NVIDIA driver. Make sure that the latest NVIDIA driver is installed and running.
```
```
NVRM: This can occur when another driver was loaded and
NVRM: obtained ownership of the NVIDIA device(s).
NVRM: Try unloading the conflicting kernel module (and/or
NVRM: reconfigure your kernel without the conflicting
NVRM: driver(s)), then try loading the NVIDIA kernel module
NVRM: again.
NVRM: No NVIDIA devices probed.
```

`nvidia.ko` also appears in `/proc/modules` for the duration of each failed load, so anything that reads loaded modules to detect the driver sees it flap.

This looks like the case in #1624, which was fixed by #1638 and then deliberately reverted by #1825/#1836. #1825 noted that #1624 "should" be re-opened, but that didn't happen. The part not covered there is the start-limit arithmetic above: the retry loop is unbounded whenever an attempt runs longer than about 1 s, which is exactly when the driver is present but unusable.

**To Reproduce**

1. On a host whose GPU is bound to `nouveau`, install the distro's NVIDIA driver with precompiled modules (here Ubuntu's `nvidia-headless-no-dkms-580-server` + `linux-modules-nvidia-580-server-generic`), and do not reboot.
2. Install `nvidia-container-toolkit` 1.20.1-1 from the stable apt repo. Its postinst enables and starts `nvidia-cdi-refresh.path` and `.service`, and the new `modules.dep` also satisfies the `ExecCondition`.
3. Run `journalctl -u nvidia-cdi-refresh.service -f` and `dmesg -w`. The service fails in `nvidia-smi -L` and restarts about every 2.3 s, with the kernel messages above each time. `systemctl show -p NRestarts nvidia-cdi-refresh.service` keeps climbing past 5.

The same shape should apply to any state where `nvidia.ko` is in `modules.dep` but the driver can't come up this boot, which is the #1624 situation.

**Expected behavior**

The unit gives up after the intended ~5 attempts, whatever each attempt's duration, or backs off, and stays failed until the next trigger (reboot, `modules.dep` change, or a manual start). Two ways this could be done, not a prescription:

- a `StartLimitIntervalSec` sized to `StartLimitBurst × (RestartSec + worst-case attempt time)`;
- `RestartSteps=`/`RestartMaxDelaySec=` (systemd ≥ 254) so retries back off.

**Workaround**

Where nothing consumes the generated spec (`/var/run/cdi/nvidia.yaml`), `systemctl mask nvidia-cdi-refresh.path nvidia-cdi-refresh.service` before installing the toolkit. The postinst leaves an administrator's mask in place.

**Environment (please provide the following information):**
 - `nvidia-container-toolkit` version: 1.20.1-1 (deb, `https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/stable/deb/amd64`); the unit, path, udev and packaging files are identical on `main` as of 84e2c2c1
 - NVIDIA Driver Version: 580.178.04 (Ubuntu `nvidia-headless-no-dkms-580-server` 580.178.04-0ubuntu0.26.04.1, precompiled modules)
 - Host OS: Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS
 - Kernel Version: 7.0.0-34-generic
 - systemd: 259 (259.5-0ubuntu3.4)
 - Container Runtime Version: not involved (the loop is the systemd unit alone)
 - CPU Architecture: `x86_64`
 - GPU Model(s): GeForce GTX 950
discussion:
I reproduced the issue in the unit configuration and found one additional compatibility wrinkle.

Making `StartLimitIntervalSec` larger alone still does not bound retries because an activation can take arbitrarily long. Using `infinity` would avoid the fixed-window reset problem on newer systemd, but it is not portable enough for the supported distro range here.

There is also an older-systemd compatibility issue: Amazon Linux 2 uses systemd 219, where the current `[Unit]` form of `StartLimitIntervalSec=` is not supported. The older `[Service]` form using `StartLimitInterval=` and `StartLimitBurst=` works there and remains accepted by newer systemd versions.

I have a small candidate that:

- moves the rate limit to the backward-compatible `[Service]` form;
- bounds each activation with `TimeoutStartSec=60s`;
- uses `StartLimitInterval=10min`, comfortably larger than `5 × (60s timeout + 1s RestartSec)`.

This makes the five-attempt limit deterministic even when `nvidia-smi -L` stalls, while still allowing a later path/udev-triggered activation after the rate-limit window expires.

Candidate diff: https://github.com/kvnloo/nvidia-container-toolkit/compare/main...fix/cdi-refresh-bounded-retries

If this direction looks reasonable, I can add the appropriate behavioral regression coverage and open the PR.

---COMMENT---

Small correction to my previous comment after tracing the packaged unit configuration more completely.

Current main already ships `10-container-engines.conf`, which applies:

`TimeoutStartSec=90s`

to `nvidia-cdi-refresh.service`.

So I removed the proposed `60s` timeout from my candidate rather than introducing a second timeout policy.

The updated candidate now:

- keeps the existing packaged `TimeoutStartSec=90s`;
- keeps `StartLimitBurst=5`;
- moves the rate-limit directives to the backward-compatible `[Service]` spelling;
- uses `StartLimitInterval=10min`;
- extends the existing systemd E2E checks to assert the effective `90s` timeout, burst, and interval together.

With the packaged defaults, five failed attempts plus `RestartSec=1s` take at most roughly:

`5 × (90s + 1s) = 455s`

which stays inside the `600s` rate-limit window, so the sixth start is deterministically rejected.

Fork validation PR:

https://github.com/kvnloo/nvidia-container-toolkit/pull/1

I'm keeping this fork-local until the direction is confirmed and the behavioral validation is sufficient.

title: nvidia-container-cli fails intermittently with "nvcgo rpc error: timed out" (hard-coded 10s RPC timeout in libnvidia-container)
error_message: nvidia-container-cli: initialization error: nvcgo rpc error: timed out
description:
**Describe the bug**

`nvidia-container-cli` intermittently fails during container startup with:

```
nvidia-container-cli: initialization error: nvcgo rpc error: timed out
```

The failure happens when the node is under CPU/IO pressure (e.g. a burst of GPU containers starting at the same time). The error is produced by the hard-coded 10 second RPC client timeout in `libnvidia-container`:

- `src/rpc.c` (`setup_client`):

```c
struct timeval timeout = {10, 0};
...
clnt_control(rpc->clt, CLSET_TIMEOUT, (char *)&timeout);
```

During `nvc_init()`, `nvcgo_init()` (`src/nvcgo.c`) forks a child process that serves an ONC RPC over a unix socketpair. The server-side handler `nvcgo_init_1_svc` `dlopen()`s the Go c-shared library `libnvcgo.so` (with `RTLD_NOW`), which boots a full Go runtime. On a loaded or slow node (cold page cache, CPU throttling, IO contention, container start storms), `fork + dlopen + Go runtime init` can exceed 10 s, so `clnt_call()` returns `RPC_TIMEDOUT` and the whole container start fails.

The timeout is hard-coded: it is not configurable via the config file, an environment variable, or a CLI flag, and there is no retry.

Note this is a different failure flavor from the well-known `driver rpc error: timed out` (#237, #202), which is caused by slow NVML initialization when persistence mode is off. The `nvcgo` RPC program only loads the Go cgroup helper library and does not touch NVML, so enabling persistence mode does not help here.

**To Reproduce**

1. Use a node under heavy CPU/IO load (or artificially slow down process spawn / file reads, e.g. cold page cache + `stress-ng`).
2. Start a GPU container (legacy mode), e.g. `docker run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.0.0-base-ubuntu22.04 nvidia-smi`, or launch a burst of GPU pods on Kubernetes with the legacy runtime mode.
3. Intermittently, container creation fails with `nvidia-container-cli: initialization error: nvcgo rpc error: timed out`.

**Expected behavior**

The nvcgo RPC initialization should be resilient to slow nodes:

- the RPC timeout should be configurable (e.g. via `nvidia-container-cli` config / env var), and/or
- the default should be more tolerant, and/or
- the call should be retried before failing the container start.

**Environment (please provide the following information):**
 - `nvidia-container-toolkit` version: v1.17.8 (also verified in the latest release v1.20.0, see below)
 - NVIDIA Driver Version: 550.x
 - Host OS: Ubuntu 22.04
 - Kernel Version: 5.15-generic
 - Container Runtime Version: containerd 1.7.x
 - CPU Architecture: x86_64
 - Kubernetes Distro and Version: K8s

**Additional context**

I verified that the issue is still present in the latest release:

- `nvidia-container-toolkit` v1.20.0 pins `third_party/libnvidia-container` at `3e428194` (libnvidia-container v1.20.0).
- In libnvidia-container v1.20.0 (and current `main`), `src/rpc.c` still contains the same hard-coded `struct timeval timeout = {10, 0}`; there were no timeout-related changes to `src/rpc.c` between v1.17.8 and v1.20.0.
- `nvcgo_init()` is called unconditionally from `nvc_init()` in builds with `WITH_NVCGO=yes` (the default for official packages), so every `nvidia-container-cli configure` invocation pays this fork+dlopen cost and is exposed to the 10 s budget.

Workarounds we are considering on our side: switch the runtime to CDI mode (which does not invoke `nvidia-container-cli`), reduce node-level start bursts. A configurable timeout would still be appreciated.

title: Support injecting POSIX rlimits (e.g. RLIMIT_MEMLOCK for RDMA) into the OCI spec via nvidia-container-runtime config
error_message: - **Scope**: this only works where `nvidia-container-runtime` is the runtime (RuntimeClass / default runtime). The `nvidia-container-runtime-hook`-only path (`docker --gpus`) cannot alter rlimits — a prestart hook runs after the process rlimits are set. Documenting that limitation seems acceptable.
missing_evidence: driver_version, cuda_version, os_info, gpu_model, repro_steps, nvidia_smi_output
description:
### Problem

RDMA workloads (GPUDirect RDMA, NCCL over IB/RoCE, UCX) need to pin buffer pools that run to gigabytes. Kubernetes never sets `RLIMIT_MEMLOCK`, so every container inherits it from the container runtime daemon — with containerd under systemd that is the 8 MiB `LimitMEMLOCK` default. `ibv_reg_mr` then fails with `ENOMEM` and NCCL silently falls back to TCP sockets.

The standard advice — add the `IPC_LOCK` capability to the pod — **only works for containers that run as root**. For a non-root container, capabilities added via `securityContext.capabilities.add` land in the bounding set but never in the effective/permitted set (Kubernetes has no ambient-capability support), so `CAP_IPC_LOCK` is silently inert.

Measured on Kubernetes 1.36 / containerd 2.3.3 / toolkit v1.19.1 (via GPU Operator), same image, same node:

| container user | `CapEff` | `ulimit -l` | `mlock` test |
|---|---|---|---|
| uid 1000 + `IPC_LOCK` added | `0000000000000000` (cap lost) | 8192 KB | 64 MiB → `ENOMEM` |
| uid 0 + `IPC_LOCK` added | `a80465fb` (cap effective) | 8192 KB | 1 GiB → OK |

Since GPU images increasingly run as non-root, there is currently **no per-runtime way** to give GPU containers a usable memlock limit:

- `LimitMEMLOCK=infinity` on the containerd systemd unit works, but is node-wide — every container on the node gets it, not just GPU workloads.
- containerd's per-runtime `base_runtime_spec` could scope it to the nvidia runtime, but it replaces the entire default OCI spec (fragile across containerd upgrades), and the toolkit option that could set it — `RUNTIME_CONFIG_OVERRIDE` — has been non-functional since the v1.17 refactor (see "Related regression" below).

### Proposal

Let `nvidia-container-runtime` — which is already an OCI-spec-rewriting shim — optionally inject POSIX rlimits into the spec:

```toml
[nvidia-container-runtime]
rlimits = ["memlock=unlimited"]        # or e.g. "memlock=1073741824:unlimited"
```

Implementation sketch (happy to submit a PR, it is small and self-contained):

1. `api/config/v1/runtime.go`: add `Rlimits []string` to `RuntimeConfig`.
2. `internal/modifier/rlimit.go` (new): an `oci.SpecModifier` that parses the entries into `specs.POSIXRlimit` and merges them into `spec.Process.Rlimits` (replace an existing entry of the same type, append otherwise). `unlimited` maps to `math.MaxUint64` (`RLIM_INFINITY` in runc).
3. `internal/modifier/factory.go`: register the modifier for all runtime modes.
4. `cmd/nvidia-ctk-installer/toolkit/toolkit.go`: a `--nvidia-container-runtime.rlimits` flag (env `NVIDIA_CONTAINER_RUNTIME_RLIMITS`) added to the existing `optionalConfigValues` map so the toolkit container can render it into the installed `config.toml`.

With (4), GPU Operator users can enable it with no operator changes via `toolkit.env`:

```yaml
toolkit:
  env:
  - name: NVIDIA_CONTAINER_RUNTIME_RLIMITS
    value: memlock=unlimited
```

Design points worth agreeing on up front:

- **Not gated on device requests**: unlike the feature-gated modifiers, this should apply to every container handled by the runtime when configured. RDMA-only pods (e.g. `rdma/…` resource, no GPU) may not set `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` yet still need the limit.
- **Merge semantics**: an entry configured here overrides a same-type rlimit already present in the spec (the config expresses administrator intent).
- **Scope**: this only works where `nvidia-container-runtime` is the runtime (RuntimeClass / default runtime). The `nvidia-container-runtime-hook`-only path (`docker --gpus`) cannot alter rlimits — a prestart hook runs after the process rlimits are set. Documenting that limitation seems acceptable.

### Prior art / why this belongs in the NVIDIA runtime

- Kubernetes has declined pod-level rlimits for a decade (kubernetes/kubernetes#3595); a KEP discussion (KEP-5758) only started in the v1.36 cycle and has not landed.
- containerd maintainers explicitly rejected a dockerd-style daemon-wide `default-ulimits` option (containerd/containerd#3150); the containerd answer is per-runtime `base_runtime_spec`, which replaces the entire default spec and is painful to maintain across containerd upgrades.
- dockerd's `default-ulimits` exists but is daemon-wide, not GPU-scoped.

`nvidia-container-runtime` is the one component in this stack that (a) already rewrites the OCI spec per container, (b) is naturally scoped to exactly the workloads that need pinned memory, and (c) is centrally configurable across a fleet via the GPU Operator.

### Related regression: `RUNTIME_CONFIG_OVERRIDE` is parsed but never applied

While investigating alternatives we found that the containerd `--runtime-config-override` flag (added in #497, worked through v1.16.x where `AddRuntime` ended with `runtimeSubtree.applyOverrides(configOverrides...)`) lost its consumer in the v1.17 `tools/container` → `cmd/nvidia-ctk-installer` refactor:

- v1.19.1: the flag is absent from the installer tree entirely.
- v1.20.0: the flag and the `runtimeConfigOverride()` helper are defined again in `cmd/nvidia-ctk-installer/container/runtime/containerd/containerd.go`, but nothing calls the helper — `Setup → Configure(cfg) → UpdateConfig(cfg) → AddRuntime(name, path, setAsDefault)` carries no override anywhere, so setting `RUNTIME_CONFIG_OVERRIDE` is a silent no-op.

Happy to split that into a separate issue if preferred.
discussion: I'm closing this one as explained in #2038. Happy to discuss the use cases and other potential opportunities. Thanks.

`nvidia-container-toolkit` injects `/run/nvidia-persistenced/socket` into the OCI spec when the NVIDIA `utility` driver capability is enabled. With the `runsc`/gVisor runtime, container creation then fails because gVisor attempts to open the already-mounted Unix-domain socket as a regular file and receives `ENXIO` (`No such device or address`).

The outer Docker error is:

```text
failed to create task for container: failed to create shim task:
OCI runtime create failed: creating container:
cannot create sandbox: cannot read client sync file:
waiting for sandbox to start: EOF
```

The actual gVisor gofer error is:

```text
FATAL ERROR: error setting up FS:
mounting {Destination:/run/nvidia-persistenced/socket
Source:/run/nvidia-persistenced/socket
Options:[nosuid nodev rbind rprivate noexec]}:
open(".../merged/run/nvidia-persistenced/socket") failed:
no such device or address
```

The relevant OCI mount injected by NVIDIA Container Toolkit is:

```json
{
  "destination": "/run/nvidia-persistenced/socket",
  "source": "/run/nvidia-persistenced/socket",
  "options": [

    "nodev",
    "rbind",

  "runtimes": {

      "path": "/usr/bin/runsc",

        "--nvproxy-allowed-driver-capabilities=all"

works, and:

title: update-application-profile hook fails container create when /etc/nvidia is read-only (v1.20.0)
error_message: failed to create application profiles directory:
description:
**Describe the bug**

The `update-application-profile` CDI hook (added in #1939, first shipped in toolkit **1.20.0**) aborts container creation when `/etc/nvidia` is a read-only mount inside the container.

The hook runs `mkdir /etc/nvidia/nvidia-application-profiles-rc.d` in the container root. If `/etc/nvidia` is read-only (e.g. a ConfigMap mounted there), the `mkdir` returns `EROFS`, the hook exits non-zero, and `createContainer` fails — so the container never starts:

```
createContainer hook #6: exit status 1, stderr:
failed to create application profiles directory:
mkdirat etc/nvidia/nvidia-application-profiles-rc.d: read-only file system
```

The hook runs for any GPU container with graphics/display caps (or `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` set), including non-graphics workloads (e.g. ML inference) that never use EGL/Vulkan. In our cluster it hit the NVIDIA k8s device plugin (which sets `--config-file=/etc/nvidia/config`, making `/etc/nvidia` a read-only ConfigMap mount) on every GPU node, so nodes stopped advertising `nvidia.com/gpu` and all GPU workloads were stuck. Same manifests worked on toolkit 1.19.x; the failure started only after the upgrade to 1.20.0.

**To Reproduce**

1. A node running toolkit 1.20.0 with the nvidia runtime as default.
2. Apply this pod — it needs **no** `nvidia.com/gpu` request; env-based injection is enough to trigger the hook, and it consumes no GPU:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: { name: ro-etc-nvidia }
data: { placeholder: "1" }          # ConfigMap mount => /etc/nvidia is read-only
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: hook-repro }
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  # schedule onto a GPU node running toolkit 1.20.0
  containers:
    - name: repro
      image: public.ecr.aws/docker/library/busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh","-c","echo ok; sleep 20"]
      env:
        - { name: NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, value: "all" }
        - { name: NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES, value: "all" }
      volumeMounts:
        - { name: ro, mountPath: /etc/nvidia, readOnly: true }
  volumes:
    - { name: ro, configMap: { name: ro-etc-nvidia } }
```

3. The pod fails immediately at container create with the error above.
4. Remove the read-only `/etc/nvidia` mount and the pod starts fine.

**Expected behavior**

The `update-application-profile` hook should not fatally abort container creation when it cannot create its directory because `/etc/nvidia` is read-only. On `EROFS` it should skip/warn rather than fail `createContainer`. An optional EGL/Vulkan graphics profile should not take down GPU containers (especially non-graphics ones) that have a read-only `/etc/nvidia`.

**Environment (please provide the following information):**
 - `nvidia-container-toolkit` version: **1.20.0** (commit `5505e2f94d9aaa08561490db974ba3cd676af209`)
 - NVIDIA Driver Version: `580.178.04`
 - Host OS: Amazon Linux 2023 (EKS-optimized AL2023 NVIDIA AMI `amazon-eks-node-al2023-x86_64-nvidia-1.34-v20260818` / `ami-08c7a4ee0ad23c32b`)
 - Kernel Version: `6.12.100-125.179.amzn2023.x86_64`
 - Container Runtime Version: `containerd 2.2.5`
 - CPU Architecture: `x86_64`
 - GPU Model(s): NVIDIA A10G (g5), L4 (g6), L40S (g6e) — all affected

 If applicable, also provide:
 - Kubernetes Distro and Version: Amazon EKS 1.34
 - NVIDIA GPU Operator version: not used — standalone `k8s-device-plugin v0.15.0`
 - CUDA Version: N/A

**Information to attach**

* Output of `nvidia-smi`: `<attach>`
* Container logs: N/A — the container never starts; the failure is at `createContainer` (error above). The repro pod reproduces it identically.

---

_Likely a regression from #1939, which introduced this hook. Related but distinct from #1899 (that was the hook being **missing** in CDI mode; this is the new hook **failing** on a read-only path)._

description:
**Question**:

what is the intended mechanism today for setting `containerd` runtime overrides when using the tookit installer?

asking since there does still appear to be a `--runtime-config-override` flag, but seems to be an unintended artifact of https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/pull/722 which followed its removal in a previous PR https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/pull/643#discussion_r1780736399 with rationale that it was unnecessary complexity.
 https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/blob/357b970814261fb17d9b4991b1d2636bce71d442/cmd/nvidia-ctk-installer/container/runtime/containerd/containerd.go#L78-L84

the "inheritance" mechanism which reads from the [default or fallback runtime](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/blob/357b970814261fb17d9b4991b1d2636bce71d442/pkg/config/engine/containerd/config.go#L36-L43) block works sufficiently well, but is tied closer to node infra/provisioning, which doesn't feel ideal for dynamic installations.

hoping to either re-introduce the `--runtime-config-override` feature or note down a recommended stance on how this should be done (and remove the dead code). maybe externally-managed containerd drop-in configs are the right way to go but then thats implicitly tied to the chosen `NVIDIA_RUNTIME_NAME` and whatnot.

```sh

nvidia-cdi-refresh.path

```sh
#Environment=NVIDIA_CTK_CDI_OUTPUT_FILE_PATH=/var/run/cdi/nvidia.yaml

description:
### Summary

After upgrading from:

- libnvidia-container 1.19.0-1
- nvidia-container-toolkit 1.19.0-1

to:

- libnvidia-container 1.19.1-1
- nvidia-container-toolkit 1.19.1-1

CUDA initialization inside Docker containers fails with:

`cuInit(0) failed -> CUDA_ERROR_UNKNOWN`

Downgrading both packages back to 1.19.0-1 fixes the issue immediately.

### Environment

OS:
- Manjaro Linux

GPU:
- NVIDIA GeForce GTX 970 (Maxwell, Compute Capability 5.2)

Driver:
- 580.173.02

Kernel:
- 6.18.39-1-MANJARO

Docker:
- cgroup v2
- systemd cgroup driver

### Host test

This succeeds:

```bash
ffmpeg \
  -hide_banner \
  -init_hw_device cuda=0 \
  -f lavfi -i testsrc \
  -frames:v 1 \
  -f null -
```

### Container reproducer

title: vendored go-nvlib is affected by tryResolveLibrary directory-shadowing bug (NVIDIA/go-nvlib#107)

description:
This repo vendors github.com/NVIDIA/go-nvlib v0.12.0 (vendor/github.com/NVIDIA/go-nvlib/pkg/nvlib/info/root.go), used from internal/info/auto.go via info.New(...) and nvinfo.ResolvePlatform().

That version has the bug from NVIDIA/go-nvlib#107: tryResolveLibrary resolves each candidate path with filepath.EvalSymlinks but never checks whether the result is a regular file. EvalSymlinks succeeds for directories too, so a stray directory named after a library in an earlier search path, for example /usr/lib64/libnvidia-ml.so.1, shadows the real library found later under /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu. Platform and library resolution here can end up pointing at a directory instead of the driver library.

The fix ("Skip non-regular files in tryResolveLibrary") is merged in NVIDIA/go-nvlib#108, but go-nvlib hasn't tagged a release past v0.12.0, so a normal go get -u won't pick it up yet.

Once go-nvlib cuts a release with #108 in it, or if a pseudo-version pin to the merge commit a9dc4f8 works as a stopgap, this repo's go.mod and vendor tree need the bump.
