title: nvcr.io advertises a different token realm after a token expires, dead-ending anonymous token refresh
error_message: When pulling from `nvcr.io` with the standard Docker Registry v2 bearer-token flow, we noticed that the token realm the registry advertises **changes across the auth lifecycle**, which leaves an anonymous client unable to refresh once its token expires.
description:
_**Important Note: NVIDIA AI Enterprise customers can get support from NVIDIA Enterprise support. Please open a case [here](https://enterprise-support.nvidia.com/s/create-case)**._

**Describe the bug**
First off, I'm not sure if this is the write repo/place to report issues with `nvcr.io`. I'd appreciate if someone could point me to the correct spot if this isn't it.

When pulling from `nvcr.io` with the standard Docker Registry v2 bearer-token flow, we noticed that the token realm the registry advertises **changes across the auth lifecycle**, which leaves an anonymous client unable to refresh once its token expires.

1. On the first request with **no token**, the registry returns `401` with a challenge whose realm is **`https://nvcr.io/proxy_auth`**.
2. Following that realm anonymously returns `200 OK` with a bearer token (a `pull` grant for public repos), and the pull succeeds.
3. When that token **expires** and the client retries, the registry returns `401` — but now the challenge points to a **different realm**, **`https://authn.nvidia.com/token`** with `service="registry"` and `error="invalid_token"`.
4. A client normally refreshes by following the realm in the challenge it just received. Following this second realm anonymously returns **`401` with no token** — whereas the first realm (`nvcr.io/proxy_auth`) still issues one. So the client, having correctly followed the advertised realm, has no way to obtain a fresh token and the pull dead-ends.

In other words, the realm advertised when unauthenticated (`nvcr.io/proxy_auth`, which issues tokens anonymously) is not the realm advertised after a token is presented and rejected (`authn.nvidia.com/token`, which does not) — so anonymous token refresh after expiry terminates on a `401`.

We also noticed the registry keeps accepting an **expired** token for a short grace window (still `200` shortly past the token's `exp`, rejected a few minutes later) — a secondary inconsistency, though the realm switch above is the part that breaks refresh.

**Expected behavior**

- The registry should advertise a **consistent token realm/`service`** across the auth lifecycle — the realm in the post-expiry `401` should be the same one advertised on the initial `401`, so a client that follows the advertised realm can obtain a fresh token and retry.
- If the intended realm is `authn.nvidia.com/token`, it should be the one advertised from the start (and it should issue tokens for anonymous pulls of public content the same way `nvcr.io/proxy_auth` does).

**To Reproduce*

```
# 1) no token -> 401, realm A = nvcr.io/proxy_auth
curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null -H "Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json" \
  https://nvcr.io/v2/nvidia/tritonserver/manifests/sha256:58df7489c3f2276f9591d500a012dee03e23d35543ce3c390b4c001e6bf90794
#   401 ; WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="https://nvcr.io/proxy_auth",scope="repository:nvidia/tritonserver:pull"

# 2) follow realm A anonymously -> 200 + token (pull grant); the pull works
curl -sS "https://nvcr.io/proxy_auth?scope=repository:nvidia/tritonserver:pull"
#   200 ; {"token":"<jwt, ~10 min lifetime>"}

# 3) after the token expires, retry -> 401, realm B = authn.nvidia.com/token (DIFFERENT)
curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null -H "Authorization: Bearer <expired token from step 2>" \
  -H "Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json" \
  https://nvcr.io/v2/nvidia/tritonserver/manifests/sha256:58df7489...
#   401 ; WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="https://authn.nvidia.com/token",service="registry",scope="repository:nvidia/tritonserver:pull",error="invalid_token"

# 4) follow realm B anonymously -> 401, no token issued (refresh dead-ends)
curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null "https://authn.nvidia.com/token?service=registry&scope=repository:nvidia/tritonserver:pull"
#   401

# (contrast) realm A still issues a token anonymously
curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null "https://nvcr.io/proxy_auth?scope=repository:nvidia/tritonserver:pull"
#   200
```

title: DGX Spark (GB10): host freezes during heavy Docker vLLM workloads (manual power cycle needed) on CDI-enabled toolkit stack; legacy-aligned stack is stable (causal factor not isolated)
error_message: - After bringing the box back, we often **could not find a clear smoking gun** in the logs: no obvious kernel panic, no helpful OOM trail, no Xid. The journal frequently **stops abruptly** around the workload.
description:
## Summary

On **NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, sm_121a)**, **heavy Docker-based vLLM workloads** (model load, FlashInfer autotune, CUDA compile, sustained inference) can push the host into a **bad state**:

- The machine **freezes or becomes completely unresponsive** (SSH dead).
- Recovery required a **manual power cycle** — not a clean `sudo reboot`.
- After bringing the box back, we often **could not find a clear smoking gun** in the logs: no obvious kernel panic, no helpful OOM trail, no Xid. The journal frequently **stops abruptly** around the workload.

Sometimes the container also appeared stuck in late loading (`shm_broadcast`, compile, autotune) before things went sideways — but the symptom that hurt most was the **whole host dying on us**, not merely a slow API bring-up.

The same workloads became **stable** after we aligned the affected host to a **legacy nvidia-container runtime stack** (CDI disabled, toolkit/docker pinned).

We have **not isolated the causal variable**: the fix changed toolkit version (1.19.1 → 1.19.0), disabled CDI, aligned Docker CE, and included a host reboot before redeploy. A second Spark in our lab was only a **stable reference** that surfaced the container-stack drift — we are **not** claiming mixed CDI/legacy across a cluster is the root cause.

**Contrast:** `llama-server` run via **systemd on the host** (no container toolkit) was stable throughout on the same machine.

Related: #1456, [ggml-org/llama.cpp#23111](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/23111)

---

## Environment

| Item | Affected node (broken) | Stable reference (discovery only) |
|------|------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| Hardware | DGX Spark / GB10 (UMA, aarch64) | DGX Spark / GB10 |
| NVIDIA driver | 580.159.03 | 580.159.03 |
| Kernel | 6.17.0-1026-nvidia | 6.17.0-1026-nvidia |
| CUDA toolkit (host) | 13.0.x | 13.0.x |
| `nvidia-container-toolkit` | **1.19.1-1** | **1.19.0-1** |
| `docker-ce` | **29.2.1** | **29.1.3** |
| `nvidia-cdi-refresh` | **enabled** | **disabled** |
| `nvidia-ctk cdi list` | **devices present** (`/var/run/cdi/nvidia.yaml`) | **empty** |
| `mode` in `/etc/nvidia-container-runtime/config.toml` | `auto` | `auto` |
| Effective `docker compose` / `gpus: all` injection | **CDI** (`docker info` showed `cdi: nvidia.com/gpu=...`) | **legacy nvidia runtime** |

---

## Workloads / symptoms

### Single-node Docker vLLM (primary case)

- Image: `ghcr.io/aeon-7/aeon-vllm-ultimate:latest` (vLLM 0.23.x, sm_121a)
- Models: Qwen3.6-27B AEON XS + DFlash (similar AEON stacks)
- Symptom: during heavy load (late model load, compile/autotune), the **host would freeze** and require **manual power cycle**. Logs after recovery were often inconclusive.
- Occasionally the container looked stuck in late loading before the host became unresponsive.
- Initially suspected vLLM tuning (`max-num-seqs`, UMA). After stack alignment below, **the same loading and inference profiles ran normally** without vLLM flag changes.

### Multi-node Docker vLLM TP=2 (secondary observation)

- DSpark / DeepSeek V4 Flash NVFP4, TP=2 across two Sparks
- Symptom: indefinite `shm_broadcast`; head container worker process at ~99% CPU; API never listened; host recovery again required **manual power cycle** in bad runs
- **Container-only restart did not recover**; host reboot + stack alignment did

### Not affected

- `llama.cpp` `llama-server` via **systemd** on the same GB10 host (direct driver, no container toolkit)

---

## What changed between broken and stable

On the affected node we applied (in one maintenance window):

```bash
# Toolkit pin
sudo apt-get install -y --allow-downgrades \
  nvidia-container-toolkit=1.19.0-1 \
  nvidia-container-toolkit-base=1.19.0-1 \
  libnvidia-container1=1.19.0-1 \
  libnvidia-container-tools=1.19.0-1

# CDI off
sudo systemctl disable --now nvidia-cdi-refresh.service nvidia-cdi-refresh.path
sudo rm -rf /var/run/cdi /etc/cdi
sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker --cdi.enabled=false

# Docker pin (to match reference node)
sudo apt-get install -y --allow-downgrades \
  docker-ce=5:29.1.3-1~ubuntu.24.04~noble \
  docker-ce-cli=5:29.1.3-1~ubuntu.24.04~noble

sudo systemctl restart docker
# + host reboot before redeploy
```

**Verify (stable state):**

```bash
nvidia-ctk cdi list                    # empty
docker info | grep -E 'Runtimes|cdi:' # legacy nvidia runtime; no cdi: devices
docker run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.0.0-base-ubuntu22.04 nvidia-smi -L
```

---

## How the broken state likely arose

Routine `apt upgrade` on the affected node pulled **`nvidia-container-toolkit` 1.19.0 → 1.19.1**, enabled **`nvidia-cdi-refresh`**, and generated a CDI spec. With `mode = "auto"`, Docker `gpus: all` used **CDI injection**. Docker CE also upgraded (29.1.3 → 29.2.1).

We did not intentionally enable CDI for experimentation — it came from package defaults after upgrade.

---

## What we cannot claim

Because we changed **multiple variables at once** (toolkit version, CDI on/off, Docker version, reboot), we **cannot** state whether the freezes were caused by:

- CDI injection path on GB10,
- `nvidia-container-toolkit` 1.19.1 specifically,
- Docker 29.2.1,
- UMA / vLLM memory pressure interacting with the container stack,
- or residual bad GPU/driver state requiring reboot.

We also **cannot** confirm that **1.19.0 + CDI** would be fine — we did not test that combination.

We are **not** claiming spontaneous unclean reboots without user intervention in every case; our consistent recovery path was **manual power cycle after the host became unresponsive**.

---

## Questions for maintainers

1. For **DGX Spark / GB10**, what is the **recommended** Docker GPU injection path for heavy workloads (CUDA compile, FlashInfer autotune, large vLLM cold start / inference): **legacy** or **CDI**?
2. Did **1.19.1** change CDI defaults or behavior vs **1.19.0** on Spark in a way that could destabilize the host under long-running GPU work inside containers?
3. Is there a known-good pinned combination (toolkit + Docker + CDI setting) for GB10 that NVIDIA validates for containerized inference?

---

## Diagnostic snapshot (broken vs stable)

```bash
dpkg -l nvidia-container-toolkit docker-ce | awk '/^ii/{print $2,$3}'
systemctl is-enabled nvidia-cdi-refresh.service
grep '^mode' /etc/nvidia-container-runtime/config.toml
nvidia-ctk cdi list
docker info | grep -E 'Runtimes|cdi:'
```

Happy to provide sanitized container logs (`shm_broadcast` stall) on request.
discussion:
Closing this report — we no longer believe the container-toolkit / CDI vs legacy stack drift explains the failures.

After aligning to the legacy stack (toolkit 1.19.0, CDI disabled, Docker pinned) and running stably for a while, the host **froze again** under heavy Docker vLLM workload and required another **manual power cycle**. That suggests the root cause is **more complex** than we originally framed (likely multiple factors: UMA pressure, vLLM/driver interaction, recovery state, etc.).

Withdrawing so we don't mislead others into thinking legacy parity is a complete fix. Sorry for the noise, and thanks to anyone who looked at this.

title: JIT-CDI graphics visibility is inconsistent on multi-GPU hosts: Vulkan works for one single-GPU pod but not another
description:
Describe the bug

On a 2-GPU host using the CDI/JIT-CDI path, two pods are created with one GPU allocated to each pod. Vulkan graphics works in the pod assigned one GPU, but fails in the pod assigned the other GPU.

From checking the Toolkit source, CDI does inject graphics files and per-GPU device nodes, including EGL/GLVND/Vulkan configs and matching /dev/dri/* nodes. However, the CDI/JIT-CDI path does not appear to create the legacy NVIDIA application profile:

/etc/nvidia/nvidia-application-profiles-rc.d/10-container.conf

That legacy file sets EGLVisibleDGPUDevices for the allocated GPU minor. Without it, NVIDIA graphics userspace appears to still make some presentation/WSI decisions from a host-global view. This can make the GPU that matches the default/global graphics view work, while the other allocated GPU fails.

A downstream patch that restores this per-container application profile for the allocated GPU minor fixes the issue.

To Reproduce

Detailed steps to reproduce the issue.

1. Use a host with 2 NVIDIA GPUs.
2. Enable Toolkit CDI/JIT-CDI mode.
3. Create two Kubernetes pods, each requesting one NVIDIA GPU.
4. Confirm each pod is assigned a different GPU.
5. In each pod, run a Vulkan WSI/presentation test, for example an app or probe that checks queue presentSupport and attempts swapchain creation.
6. Compare the two pods.

Observed result:

- The pod assigned one GPU works with Vulkan.
- The pod assigned the other GPU fails Vulkan presentation/swapchain support.
- The failing pod has a selected GPU device set, but no /etc/nvidia/nvidia-application-profiles-rc.d/10-container.conf.

Expected behavior

Each pod allocated one full GPU through CDI/JIT-CDI should get a coherent one-GPU graphics view. Vulkan presentation and swapchain creation should work regardless of which physical GPU/minor the pod receives.

Environment
nvidia-container-toolkit version: [v1.19.1]
NVIDIA Driver Version: [580.82.07]
Host OS: [Ubuntu 24.04]
Kernel Version: [6.8.0-generic]
CPU Architecture: [x86_64]
GPU Model(s): [GeForce-RTX-5070-Ti]
discussion:
Looking at the current CDI/CDI-JIT implementation, nvidia application profile isn't created in the CDI code path. In the legacy mode, the profile is created when the container has the "graphics/display" capability. Maybe we can add a hook to create the profile for CDI use cases?

@cdesiniotis WDYT?

@tzmtl I have a patch #1939 that's able to generate the nvidia application profiles for CDI/JIT-CDI scenarios. Will you be able to help with validating this fix in your environment?

---COMMENT---

Well, if the root cause is missing the nvidia application profile, this patch should fix it.

Two questions:
* Do you see `/etc/nvidia/nvidia-application-profiles-rc.d/10-container.conf` in the container?
* Are you using CDI mode or JIT-CDI mode? If using CDI, the CDI spec needs to be re-generated by the updated nvidia-ctk. But yes, if spec is generated by the k8s-device-plugin, it would also require an update too.

description:
**Describe the bug**

When `toolkit.installDir` is set to a non-standard location (required for OSes with a read-only `/usr`), `nvidia-container-cli` is installed to a path like `/opt/nvidia/toolkit/nvidia-container-cli`. This path is not on the system or containerd `$PATH`.

gVisor's `runsc` uses `exec.LookPath("nvidia-container-cli")` to locate the binary ([source](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/master/runsc/container/container.go) — see `nvProxyPreGoferHostSetup`), which fails with:

```
failed to locate nvidia-container-cli in PATH:
exec: "nvidia-container-cli": executable file not found in $PATH
```

This works with runc because `nvidia-container-runtime` resolves the binary path from its own config TOML. gVisor intentionally does not parse that config ([source](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/cb94f02180f4/runsc/container/container.go#L2090-L2098)) and relies on standard PATH lookup instead.

**To Reproduce**

1. GPU Operator installs toolkit DaemonSet with `toolkit.installDir` set to a non-default path (e.g. `/opt/nvidia/toolkit/`).
2. gVisor/runsc is configured as an alternative runtime with `nvproxy: true`.
3. A GPU pod with `runtimeClassName: gvisor` fails to start because `runsc` calls `exec.LookPath("nvidia-container-cli")` during container creation, and the binary is not on the inherited PATH.

**Expected behavior**

`nvidia-container-cli` should be discoverable via standard PATH lookup after toolkit installation, regardless of `installDir`. Note that the motivation for using a non-default `installDir` is that `/usr` is read-only on these OSes, so symlinking into `/usr/local/bin` is not a viable solution.

**Workaround**

Extend containerd's PATH via a systemd drop-in:
```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/containerd.service.d/nvidia-toolkit.conf
[Service]
Environment=PATH=/opt/nvidia/toolkit:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
```
Followed by `systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart containerd`.

**Environment:**
 - `nvidia-container-toolkit` version: v1.17.4 (also reproduced with v1.19.1)
 - NVIDIA Driver Version: 590.48.01 (open kernel modules)
 - Host OS: Garden Linux 2150.4 (read-only `/usr`)
 - Container Runtime Version: containerd 2.0.x
 - CPU Architecture: x86_64
 - GPU Model(s): T4
 - Kubernetes: 1.31
 - NVIDIA GPU Operator version: 24.9.2
 - gVisor/runsc version: release-20260511.0
discussion:
What's your suggestion here @Vincinator ?

---COMMENT---

When `toolkit.installDir` is set to a non-default path, the toolkit should ensure `installDir` is on containerd's PATH, for example by installing a systemd drop-in:

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/containerd.service.d/nvidia-toolkit-path.conf
[Service]
Environment="PATH=/opt/nvidia/toolkit:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin"
```

This way, any binary that containerd spawns (including `runsc`) inherits the correct PATH and can locate `nvidia-container-cli` via standard lookup.

This requires a `daemon-reload` followed by a service restart to take effect. The toolkit already supports restarting the runtime service via [systemd restart mode](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/blob/59c042086ec2/cmd/nvidia-ctk-installer/container/runtime/containerd/containerd.go#L138-L140), so adding a `daemon-reload` before that restart seems like a natural fit.

On the UX side, this could be gated behind a configuration option so it only takes effect when needed. But that's an implementation detail.

---COMMENT---

This issue is stale because it has been open 90 days with no activity. This issue will be closed in 30 days unless new comments are made or the stale label is removed. To skip these checks, apply the "lifecycle/frozen" label.

---COMMENT---

This affects the default `installDir` too, not only custom ones. The installer default is `/usr/local/nvidia`, so the CLI lands in `/usr/local/nvidia/toolkit/` (`cmd/nvidia-ctk-installer/main.go`), which isn't on systemd's default PATH either. runsc finds the CLI with `exec.LookPath`, using the PATH it inherits from containerd (`nvProxyPreGoferHostSetup` in `runsc/container/container.go`). It does this with the CDI hook as well, not just in legacy mode.

Having the installer write the systemd drop-in has a few problems:
- The installer restarts containerd with a signal by default, so it would need a new `daemon-reload` + systemd restart path just for this.
- `Environment=` doesn't expand `$PATH`, so the drop-in has to hardcode the full PATH and would override whatever the distro's unit sets.
- `installDir` ends up inside a unit file, so it needs escaping (`%`, newlines), and the file has to be removed on uninstall.

Options I see:

1. Fix it in gVisor (my preference). Add a runsc flag for the CLI path (e.g. `--nvproxy-cli-path`), set through `runsc_config` in the runsc shim config, where `nvproxy` is already set. The installer doesn't write anything new on the host, and it works for any `installDir` and containerd version. runsc has no such option today.
2. Toolkit, opt-in. On containerd 2.x, the installer sets `PATH` in `[plugins."io.containerd.shim.v1.manager"] env`, inside the config drop-in it already writes and reverts. That avoids systemd files, but it only works on containerd 2.0+ and changes PATH for every shim.
3. Docs only. Document the workaround.

Maintainers, does the gVisor route sound right to you, or would you rather have option 2 in the installer? I can send the gVisor PR, or implement option 2 here if you prefer.

@Vincinator, were you planning to send a PR yourself? Also, how do your runsc pods get GPUs: the legacy hook, the CDI hook, or `--nvproxy-docker`? I'm asking because runsc could fall back to the directory of the NVIDIA hook binary in the spec, and that only works when the hook is present.

---COMMENT---

I checked the current gVisor side of this as well.

`runsc/container/container.go` still resolves the CLI with:

`exec.LookPath("nvidia-container-cli")`

and the surrounding comment explicitly says runsc does not consume `/etc/nvidia-container-runtime/config.toml`.

That makes me lean toward fixing this at the gVisor boundary rather than having the toolkit mutate containerd's global/systemd `PATH`.

A small gVisor contract could be:

- add an explicit nvproxy CLI-path option, e.g. `--nvproxy-cli-path`;
- empty/default value preserves the current `exec.LookPath` behavior;
- an explicit path bypasses PATH lookup;
- expose it through the existing `runsc_config` path where `nvproxy` is already configured;
- test explicit valid path, missing path, and default lookup.

That works for both the toolkit's default install location and arbitrary `installDir` values without changing the PATH inherited by every shim.

Unless toolkit maintainers prefer option 2 here, I think the next concrete contribution belongs in `google/gvisor`.

title: nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:12.6.3-devel-ubuntu22.04 (aarch64/sbsa) does not include libibverbs.so, preventing NCCL from using IB/RoCE transport
error_message: NCCL INFO Failed to open libibverbs.so[.1]         ← root cause
description:
Image: nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:12.6.3-devel-ubuntu22.04 (pulled on aarch64/sbsa ARM64 servers)

  Cluster: RKE2 v1.35.4+rke2r1, GPU Operator v26.3.2, NVIDIA A2 GPUs, Mellanox ConnectX-6 Dx (BlueField-2 DPU), Ubuntu 22.04.5 (kernel 5.15.0-181)

  How we invoke it:
  containers:
  - image: nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:12.6.3-devel-ubuntu22.04
    resources:
      limits:
        nvidia.com/gpu: "1"
    securityContext:
      capabilities:
        add: ["IPC_LOCK"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: infiniband
      mountPath: /dev/infiniband    # host /dev/infiniband mounted
    - name: shm
      mountPath: /dev/shm
    env:
    - name: NCCL_IB_DISABLE
      value: "0"
    - name: NCCL_IB_HCA
      value: "mlx5_0:1,mlx5_1:1"
    - name: NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX
      value: "3"

  Host RDMA setup: IB devices visible at /sys/class/infiniband/mlx5_0 and mlx5_1. RoCEv2 GID index 3 = ::ffff:10.25.0.1 (IPv4-mapped, confirmed via sysfs). Raw RDMA bandwidth confirmed at 24.51 Gbps via
  ib_write_bw on the host. nvidia-peermem kernel module loaded.

  Symptom (NCCL_DEBUG=INFO output inside the container):
  NCCL INFO NET/Plugin: Could not find: libnccl-net.so. Using internal network plugin.
  NCCL INFO NCCL_IB_DISABLE set by environment to 0.
  NCCL INFO Failed to open libibverbs.so[.1]         ← root cause
  NCCL INFO Using network Socket                      ← silently falls back to TCP

  Expected: libibverbs.so.1 should either be bundled in the CUDA devel image or the NCCL package (libnccl2) should depend on libibverbs1 so apt-get install libnccl2 pulls it automatically.

  Actual: Neither the CUDA image nor the NCCL package declares a dependency on libibverbs1. NCCL silently falls back to TCP socket transport, making RDMA benchmarks appear to work while actually running over
  TCP — with no warning unless NCCL_DEBUG=INFO is set.

  Workaround: Either apt-get install libibverbs1 (which is not pulled by any existing dependency) or mount the host's libibverbs at /host-rdma-libs and set LD_LIBRARY_PATH. Prefer a proper fix so the CUDA
  image is RDMA-capable out of the box.

  Note for NVIDIA support: On x86_64, MOFED typically provides libibverbs.so system-wide, so this gap is often not noticed. On aarch64/sbsa with inbox kernel mlx5 drivers (no MOFED), the container has no path
   to get libibverbs.so without explicit installation.

  ---
  The key is either: (1) add libibverbs1 to the CUDA devel image for sbsa, or (2) make libnccl2 declare a dependency on it so it's installed automatically.
discussion: Hi @abonillabeeche, I believe the guidance here would be to include `libibverbs.so` in your container image (by either installing it yourself or building on top of a base image that includes it). Including `libibverb.so` in the CUDA devel images is likely out-of-scope as `libibverbs` is not a part of CUDA.

sudo nvidia-ctk cdi generate --feature-flag no-additional-gids-for-device-nodes
```

title: Ship static busybox shell in nvidia-container-toolkit image
missing_evidence: toolkit_version, driver_version, cuda_version, container_runtime, gpu_model, repro_steps, nvidia_smi_output
description:
Part of NVIDIA/cloud-native-team#299.

NVIDIA STIG policy is dropping `-dev` distroless tags as approved
parent images. To move the nvidia-container-toolkit image onto a
non-`-dev` base **without changing `entrypoint.sh` or any Kubernetes
manifests**, we ship a static busybox shell inside the image.

## Approach

Add a `debian:trixie-slim` shell-builder stage to
`deployments/container/Dockerfile` that apt-installs `busybox-static`.
COPY `/bin/busybox` into the final stage(s) and run
`busybox --install -s /bin` to populate `/bin/sh`, `/bin/rm`,
`/bin/ln`, etc. Flip both the `packaging` and `application` final
stages from `nvcr.io/nvidia/distroless/go:<ver>-dev` to the matching
non-`-dev` variant. Drop the existing `SHELL ["/busybox/sh", "-c"]`
directives and the `RUN ln -s /busybox/sh /bin/sh` symlinks — the
static busybox install replaces them.

```dockerfile
FROM debian:trixie-slim AS shell-builder
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install --no-install-recommends -y busybox-static \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

FROM nvcr.io/nvidia/distroless/go:<version>
COPY --from=shell-builder /bin/busybox /bin/busybox
RUN ["/bin/busybox", "--install", "-s", "/bin"]
```

The existing `entrypoint.sh` and all `nvidia-ctk-installer`
invocations remain untouched.

Precedent:
[`kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-nvidia-gpu`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-nvidia-gpu)
uses the same pattern with `bash-static`.

## Tracking

No PR yet — separate companion PR will be opened against this repo.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Both stages no longer reference `-dev` distroless tags
- [ ] No `/busybox/sh` references remain; `/bin/sh` is provided by static busybox
- [ ] Image builds successfully on amd64 and arm64
- [ ] `nvidia-ctk-installer` and the existing `entrypoint.sh`
      continue to run when consumed by gpu-operator

title: CDI pass through nvidia-ctk & nvidia-cdi-hook (dind)
description:
**What I'm doing:** For a CI runner, I need to run containers inside the runner container.
On K8S, I have a pod with a runner container and a "dind" (docker in docker, actually using podman) container.

**What I figured:** When using the CDI, `nvidia-ctk` and `nvidia-cdi-hook` mount a lot of stuff into containers, which is great so I can have nvidia-smi and cuda. But why not mount the nvidia-container-toolkit binaries ?

**workaround**:

```sh
sudo docker run -it --rm --gpus all --privileged \
	-v /usr/bin/nvidia-ctk:/usr/bin/nvidia-ctk \
	-v /usr/bin/nvidia-cdi-hook:/usr/bin/nvidia-cdi-hook \
	quay.io/podman/stable sh -c 'nvidia-smi && nvidia-ctk cdi generate --output=/etc/cdi/nvidia.yaml && podman run -it --rm --gpus all ubuntu nvidia-smi'
```
discussion:
The intent of the NVIDIA Container Toolkit is to ensure that the user-mode components of the NVIDIA GPU Driver and device nodes required for accessing NVIDIA GPUs are available to workload containers. This is required because of the explicit match required between user-mode and kernel-mode drivers. The NVIDIA Container Toolkit does NOT have this restriction and can be included in the container image to start with, for example.

---COMMENT---

Anyways I'm OK with the mount, even if I would like the option to add optional additions

title: Test Suite Fails to Lookup nvidiaRuntime in PATH
description:
**Describe the bug**
When building the runtime in a [mock](https://github.com/rpm-software-management/mock) environment the tests are failing to pass. This appears to be due to a reliance on the just-built runtime being in `PATH`.

**To Reproduce**
https://github.com/damaestro/nct-build-env

**Expected behavior**
The full test suite runs.

**Environment (please provide the following information):**
 - `nvidia-container-toolkit` version: `1.19.0`
 - NVIDIA Driver Version: `580.142` (unrelated as this is at build time)
 - Host OS: Fedora Rawhide

The attached patch is required to skip the tests that would otherwise fail.

[nvidia-container-toolkit-skip-tests.patch](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26632955/nvidia-container-toolkit-skip-tests.patch)

This is a continuation of https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/issues/794
discussion:
I am not familiar with this build environment. Do you know why https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/blob/ee31ca2762fd47229ee7f1a6f6a3e36de0618b9d/cmd/nvidia-container-runtime/main_test.go#L52 doesn't work in this environment? IIUC the runtime-under-test should be added to the `PATH`.

---COMMENT---

 The `%gobuild` macro (used in `%build`) writes binaries to `%{gobuilddir}`, which expands to `_build/bin/`
  relative to the source tree — i.e.:

```
  /builddir/build/BUILD/nvidia-container-toolkit-1.19.0-build/
    nvidia-container-toolkit-1.19.0/
      _build/bin/          ← %{gobuilddir}, where %build puts binaries
        nvidia-container-runtime      ✓ built here
        nvidia-container-runtime-hook ✓
        nvidia-cdi-hook               ✓
        ...
      tests/bin/           ← where main_test.go looks for binaries at runtime
        nvidia-container-runtime-hook ✓ (pre-existing test fixture)
        runc                          ✓ (pre-existing test fixture/mock)
        nvidia-container-runtime      ✗ MISSING
```

1.   `%build` runs `%gobuild -o %{gobuilddir}/bin/$(basename $cmd) ... for each cmd/*`. This puts `nvidia-container-runtime` into `_build/bin/`.
2.   `%install` copies `_build/bin/*` to `%{buildroot}%{_bindir}` (i.e., `BUILDROOT/usr/bin/`). The binary now exists in the staged install root, but that directory is only for packaging — not on `$PATH` during `%check`.
3.   `%check` runs `%gotest ./...` from within the source tree. The test's TestMain sets PATH to include `tests/bin/` — but nvidia-container-runtime was never placed there.

---COMMENT---

I've gone ahead and copied the staged binary from the `%build` step into the expected `tests/bin` location so we can run the tests without the patch.

I'd still like to understand if there is improvements to the tests to work better in this situation or if copying in the just-built asset is the best way forward.

Thanks!

---COMMENT---

I believe copying the just-built `nvidia-container-runtime` binary to the `tests/bin` directory or the project root is the best path forward. The `cmd/nvidia-container-runtime/main_test.go` file assumes that the just-built `nvidia-container-runtime` binary is present at one of these directories (as noted earlier, both the project root and the `tests/bin` directory get added to the `PATH` here: https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/blob/ee31ca2762fd47229ee7f1a6f6a3e36de0618b9d/cmd/nvidia-container-runtime/main_test.go#L52). Our [test](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/blob/2c0c91d0ebaa45873d997b42beffad3706e8d734/Makefile#L124) make target depends on the [cmds](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/blob/2c0c91d0ebaa45873d997b42beffad3706e8d734/Makefile#L68) target which compiles all of the Go executables in the project and creates executable files at the project root directory.

  containerPath: /usr/share/egl/egl_external_platform.d/09_nvidia_wayland2.json

description:
**Describe the bug**

CUDA initialization fails **inside containers only**, while the same host can use NVENC successfully outside containers.

The key symptom is:

- `nvidia-smi` works inside the container
- FFmpeg inside the container shows `h264_nvenc` and `cuda`
- but actual CUDA initialization fails with:

```text
cuInit(0) failed -> CUDA_ERROR_UNKNOWN: unknown error
```

I first noticed this with Plex in Docker, but I can reproduce the same failure with a plain FFmpeg container, so this does **not** appear to be Plex-specific.

---

**To Reproduce**

1. Verify the host GPU works:

```bash
nvidia-smi -L
```

2. Verify host FFmpeg NVENC works:

```bash
ffmpeg -hide_banner -encoders | grep nvenc
ffmpeg -hide_banner -decoders | grep cuvid
ffmpeg -hide_banner -hwaccels
ffmpeg -hide_banner -f lavfi -i testsrc=size=1280x720:rate=30 -t 5 -c:v h264_nvenc -f null -
```

On the host, this completes successfully.

3. Verify basic GPU visibility in containers:

```bash
docker run --rm --runtime=nvidia --gpus all ubuntu nvidia-smi
```

4. Reproduce the failure in a plain FFmpeg container:

```bash
docker run --rm \
  --runtime=nvidia \
  --gpus all \
  --entrypoint /bin/bash \
  -e NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=all \
  -e NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=compute,video,utility \

  --set accept-nvidia-visible-devices-envvar-when-unprivileged=true
```

2. Generate management CDI specs:

```bash
nvidia-ctk cdi generate --mode=management --vendor=nvidia.com --class=mig-config \
  --output=/var/run/cdi/nvidia-mig-config.yaml
nvidia-ctk cdi generate --mode=management --vendor=nvidia.com --class=mig-monitor \
  --output=/var/run/cdi/nvidia-mig-monitor.yaml
```
discussion:
How is the device plugin container given access to the GPUs. I assume that this is done by setting the default runtime for the container engine that you're using to `nvidia` and ensuring that the NVIDIA Container Toolkit is installed. As you correctly point out, the generated CDI specs do not include the MIG monitor and MIG config devices since the specs generated by default do not include management specs (which SHOULD include these device nodes). The other issue is that the new `jit-cdi` mode of the NVIDIA Container Runtime does not properly inject these devices -- which should be addressed.

In order to mitigate this, you SHOULD be able to do the following:
1. Generate a mangement CDI spec:
```
sudo nvidia-ctk cdi generate --mode=management \
    --vendor=management.nvidia.com \
    --output=/var/run/cdi/management-nvidia.yaml
```
2. Update the device plugin to request the management CDI device by setting `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=management.nvidia.com/gpu=all` in its podspec. This should trigger the injection of the correct device nodes into the device plugin container.

title: nvidia-ctk cdi generate: libdxcore.so not found on WSL2 despite being present
error_message: level=warning msg="Could not locate libdxcore.so: pattern libdxcore.so not found"
description:
## Description

`nvidia-ctk cdi generate` on WSL2 correctly auto-detects WSL mode but fails to locate `libdxcore.so`, logging:

```
level=warning msg="Could not locate libdxcore.so: pattern libdxcore.so not found"
```

The library IS present on the system at `/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libdxcore.so` and is registered in ldconfig:

```
$ ldconfig -p | grep dxcore
libdxcore.so (libc6,x86-64) => /usr/lib/wsl/lib/libdxcore.so
```

Without `libdxcore.so` in the CDI spec, NVML initialization fails inside containers with `Failed to initialize NVML: N/A`, because `libdxcore.so` bridges the Linux NVML API to the Windows DirectX GPU Kernel via `/dev/dxg`.

## Environment

- **OS**: Windows WSL2 (Linux 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2)
- **GPU**: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Laptop GPU
- **Driver**: NVIDIA 595.71, CUDA 13.2
- **nvidia-container-toolkit**: installed from nvidia apt repo (bundled in OpenShell cluster image)
- **libdxcore.so locations**:
  - `/usr/lib/wsl/lib/libdxcore.so` (WSL mount)
  - `/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libdxcore.so` (symlink/copy in gateway container)

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run on WSL2 with NVIDIA GPU
2. `nvidia-ctk cdi generate --output=/tmp/nvidia.yaml`
3. Observe warning: `"Could not locate libdxcore.so: pattern libdxcore.so not found"`
4. Inspect generated CDI spec — `libdxcore.so` not in mounts
5. Start a container using the CDI spec
6. `nvidia-smi` inside container fails: `Failed to initialize NVML: N/A`

## Expected Behavior

`nvidia-ctk cdi generate` should find `libdxcore.so` at `/usr/lib/wsl/lib/libdxcore.so` (or via ldconfig) and include it in the CDI spec mounts.

## Workaround

Manually add `libdxcore.so` to the generated CDI spec:

```yaml
# Add to containerEdits.mounts:
- hostPath: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libdxcore.so
  containerPath: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libdxcore.so
  options:
    - ro
    - nosuid
    - nodev
    - rbind
    - rprivate
```

And add `--folder /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu` to the `update-ldcache` hook args.

After this fix plus setting `mode = "cdi"` in the nvidia container runtime config, `nvidia-smi` and NVML work correctly inside containers on WSL2.

## Impact

This bug breaks the entire NVIDIA k8s device plugin stack on WSL2 when using CDI mode, since the device plugin requires NVML initialization which depends on `libdxcore.so`.

title: nvidia-cdi-refresh.service excessively broad ordering constraint
error_message: In general, ordering dependencies shipped in a package should be as minimal as possible to make the service work. A user can always add a drop-in for the unit that adds additional ordering constraints if their system requires it, but users cannot create a drop-in to remove ordering constraints that are shipped in the main unit file.
description:
**Describe the bug**
In the 1.19.0 release, a new `After=multi-user.target` requirement was added to `nvidia-cdi-refresh.service`. This new ordering dependency makes it impossible to start any unit as part of `multi-user.target` that depends on `nvidia-cdi-refresh.service` as it creates an ordering cycle in systemd. I expect this is a fairly common use-case where systemd is used to start containers that require the toolkit on boot.

It was added as part of a "fix" for https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/issues/1611. In that issue, it is notable that there doesn't seem to be any explanation as to _why_ this dependency resolves the problem. The reporter's hastily self-tested workaround was just taken at face value and added to the unit file.

In general, ordering dependencies shipped in a package should be as minimal as possible to make the service work. A user can always add a drop-in for the unit that adds additional ordering constraints if their system requires it, but users cannot create a drop-in to remove ordering constraints that are shipped in the main unit file.

**To Reproduce**
Update to the 1.19.0 version
```
► rpm -q nvidia-container-toolkit{,-base}
nvidia-container-toolkit-1.19.0-1.x86_64
nvidia-container-toolkit-base-1.19.0-1.x86_64
```

Create and enable a service that has an `After=nvidia-cdi-refresh.service` dependency, and whose `Install` section specifies `WantedBy=multi-user.target`. For example:
```
► sudo systemctl cat podman-compose.service
# /etc/systemd/system/podman-compose.service
[Unit]
Description=podman-compose in /home/bryce/Software/podman-compose
Requires=nvidia-cdi-refresh.service
After=nvidia-cdi-refresh.service

[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStartPre=-/usr/bin/podman compose -f /home/bryce/Software/podman-compose/compose.yaml up --no-start
ExecStartPre=/usr/bin/podman compose -f /home/bryce/Software/podman-compose/compose.yaml start
ExecStart=/usr/bin/podman compose -f /home/bryce/Software/podman-compose/compose.yaml wait
ExecStop=/usr/bin/podman compose -f /home/bryce/Software/podman-compose/compose.yaml down -t 30

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

On boot, systemd will flag an ordering cycle and one of the units will not be started in an effort to break that cycle.
```
Mar 15 20:06:02 magichead systemd[1]: multi-user.target: Found ordering cycle on podman-compose.service/start
Mar 15 20:06:02 magichead systemd[1]: multi-user.target: Found dependency on nvidia-cdi-refresh.service/start
Mar 15 20:06:02 magichead systemd[1]: multi-user.target: Found dependency on multi-user.target/start
Mar 15 20:06:02 magichead systemd[1]: multi-user.target: Job podman-compose.service/start deleted to break ordering cycle starting with multi-user.target/start
```

**Expected behavior**
The shipped unit file should not include dependencies unless there is a real and verifiable reason for them. For example, if this unit requires a file on a particular file system, then adding a `RequiresMountsFor` is appropriate. If it requires the Nvidia kernel module to be loaded before it starts, then perhaps an `ExecStartPre` that calls `modprobe` would be appropriate. However, adding `After=multi-user.target` is too broad of a dependency to add, even if it happens to handle both of the example requirements above because it also forces the system to wait for a bunch of other stuff that the service does not actually need.

**Environment (please provide the following information):**

title: Add dlopen locator for better NIX integration
missing_evidence: toolkit_version, driver_version, cuda_version, container_runtime, gpu_model, error_or_logs, repro_steps, nvidia_smi_output
description:
The NIX package for the NVIDIA Container Toolkit adds a library locator that uses dlopen to attempt to locate libraries: https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/blob/1c415018b24020442ee94e6b84a8a4a24078a61e/pkgs/by-name/nv/nvidia-container-toolkit/0001-Add-dlopen-discoverer.patch#L50

In order to provide better support for NIX, we should consider adding such a locator -- at least for certain types of libraries.

This was already done in https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/pull/1646 but removed again in https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/pull/1676 due to instability.

One option would be to allow the types of locators used for libraries to be configurable. See
* https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/commit/f62813c5064c97f2ef9992cddb00e4b9ecc22af8
* https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/commit/c1af7f53941433c3fa7f2cbb9f480eda378af866
discussion:
> In order to provide better support for NIX, we should consider adding such a locator -- at least for certain types of libraries.

Would you be able to explain why this is needed for NIX? Admittedly I am not very familiar with NIX.

---COMMENT---

I ran into this while bumping the package to 1.19.1 in nixpkgs (NixOS/nixpkgs#534577), so here's what's happening on the Nix side.

NixOS doesn't have a normal `/usr/lib` or a populated `ld.so.cache`. Everything lives under `/nix/store/...`, and the NVIDIA driver libs get surfaced to apps through a single symlink dir, `/run/opengl-driver/lib`, which is baked into the binary's RUNPATH at build time. That's how `nvidia-ctk` itself is linked.

So the usual FHS-path and ldcache lookups come up empty for the driver libs, even though they load fine at runtime via the RUNPATH. dlopen bridges that, it hands the lookup to the dynamic linker, which resolves them, and `dlinfo(RTLD_DI_ORIGIN)` gives back the real path to mount.

The configurable-locator direction you've already started in f62813c / c1af7f5 looks like it'd cover this. Glad to help test the Nix side if it's useful...

---COMMENT---

Ran into this on NixOS with containerd (toolkit 1.20.1 from nixpkgs, driver 580.173.02). With `mode = "auto"` every container create carrying NVIDIA env fails with:

```
failed to create the automatic CDI modifier: failed to generate CDI spec for mode "auto": … failed to get libcuda.so parent directory: failed to locate versioned driver libraries: dlopen lib*.so.580.173.02 failed
lib*.so.580.173.02: not found
```

(The first of those two lines comes from a locator patch nixpkgs carries; on a vanilla build only the second appears.)

The failing call is `Driver.updateInfo()` in `internal/lookup/root/root.go`, which passes a glob to the library locator:

```go
versionedDriverLibPaths, err := r.Libraries().Locate("lib*.so." + version)
```

dlopen can't expand a glob, so even a perfect dlopen locator can never satisfy this call site. On NixOS all legs of `NewLibraryLocator` come up empty for it (dlopen: glob; the FHS paths: the driver is under /run/opengl-driver/lib; ldcache: none on NixOS). Fixing auto mode probably needs either a glob-capable path into `updateInfo` or library search paths exposed to the runtime.

The second option is half-built: `nvcdi.WithLibrarySearchPaths` exists and `nvidia-ctk` passes it (`cdi generate --library-search-path`), but `newAutomaticCDISpecModifier` (`internal/modifier/cdi.go`) never does, and the runtime config has no such key. That is also why a static spec works fine on NixOS; `mode = "cdi"` against one is what we run now, device plugin and dcgm-exporter healthy on both hosts since.

title: NVIDIA Container Runtime ignores Docker Swarm generic GPU resource assignments
description:
**Description of the issue**

When running containers in Docker Swarm mode using generic GPU resources, Docker Swarm correctly assigns distinct GPU UUIDs to each replica, but NVIDIA Container Runtime ignores this assignment and exposes all GPUs to every container. As a result, multiple containers scheduled on the same node end up using the same physical GPU (GPU 0), leading to memory oversubscription and OOM failures.

**Steps to reproduce**

- Configure NVIDIA Container Toolkit for Docker:

```
nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker
systemctl restart docker
```

this result in my environment of following daemon.json

```
{
    "default-runtime": "nvidia",
    "default-shm-size": "1G",
    "default-ulimits": {
        "memlock": {
            "hard": -1,
            "name": "memlock",
            "soft": -1
        },
        "stack": {
            "hard": 67108864,
            "name": "stack",
            "soft": 67108864
        }
    },
    "node-generic-resources": [
        "NVIDIA-GPU=GPU-f2ba9cd4-6f6b-860f-3c78-4a6639e4b5db",
        "NVIDIA-GPU=GPU-f12d79c4-d485-2fd1-ca2d-cd5eef76fe40"
    ],
    "runtimes": {
        "nvidia": {
            "args": [],
            "path": "nvidia-container-runtime"
        }
    }
}
```
- configure nvidia-container-runtime  /etc/nvidia-container-runtime/config.toml as follow
```

#accept-nvidia-visible-devices-envvar-when-unprivileged = true

- Deploy a Swarm service requesting one GPU per replica:

As part of the build process we produce a `packaging` image that includes the
`.deb` and `.rpm` package for supported platforms. In order to test a specific
build, these can be extracted from the image and installed on the local machine.

(This is also the mechanims used to install the components of the NVIDIA
Container Toolkit in our e2e tests).

## Extract the packages:

We can extract the packages from the required packaging image by running:
```
cache=$(mktemp -d)
docker run --rm \
    -v "${cache}:/cache" \
    -w "/cache" \
    -u "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
    --entrypoint="sh" \
    ghcr.io/nvidia/container-toolkit:6a263422-packaging \
    -c "cp -rp /artifacts/packages ."
```

This will create the following folders in the `${cache}` folder on the host:
```
ls ${cache}/packages
centos7     ubuntu18.04
```

## Install the package
For debian-based systems, use the `ubuntu18.04` packages of the required architecture, and
for systems that use the RPM package manager use the `centos7` packages.

For example:
```
cd ${cache}/packages/ubuntu18.04/amd64
```

The following packages can then be installed:
```
sudo dpkg -i \
    libnvida-container1_*.deb \
    libnvida-container-tools_*.deb \
    nvidia-container-toolkit-base_*.deb \
    nvidia-container-toolkit_*.deb
```

## Cleaning Up

Note that these packages represent an UNQUALIFIED version of the NVIDIA Container Toolkit
and should not be used for production purposes. It is also recommended that these packages
be uninstalled and replaced with versions available from a public package repository.
